# Moonbirds

## Overview

Moonbirds is a collection of 10,000 pixel-art owl profile-picture (PFP) NFTs on Ethereum (ERC-721), launched in mid-April 2022 by PROOF, the company behind the members-only PROOF Collective founded by internet entrepreneur Kevin Rose. Minting cost 2.5 ETH (roughly $7,000 at the time) and access to the public sale ran through a raffle that required 2.5 ETH in a registered wallet; of the 10,000 supply, 2,000 were reserved for PROOF Collective members (two per member), 7,875 went to the public raffle, and 125 were held back by PROOF for collaborations and marketing. The launch was one of the largest of the 2022 cycle: about $280M in total sales volume within two days ($290M within four), briefly putting Moonbirds ahead of Bored Ape Yacht Club and Mutant Ape Yacht Club in trading volume.

The collection introduced "nesting," a staking-style mechanic in which holders lock a Moonbird (making it unsellable while nested) to accrue tier upgrades from Straw up to Diamond Nest (0–180 days) and earn holder rewards such as trait-based drops and the Oddities companion collection. The artwork is rendered "in-chain" — images are output directly from the Ethereum smart contracts rather than stored on IPFS. In August 2022 Rose moved Moonbirds and Oddities art to a CC0 public-domain license, and the same month PROOF raised a $50M Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), with participation from Seven Seven Six, Collab+Currency, Flamingo DAO, SV Angel and VaynerFund (Alexis Ohanian's Seven Seven Six had already invested $10M in April 2022).

Each Moonbird combines traits across eight published categories (Background, Beak, Body, Eyes, Eyewear, Feathers, Headwear, Outerwear); one catalog source counts 126 distinct trait values in total, with individual birds carrying 3–8 traits. The rarest tier is four "grail" variants — Cosmic, Enlightened, Glitch and Jade — with only 6 of each (24 birds total), each paired with a matching exclusive background (Cosmic Purple, Enlightened Purple, Glitch Red, Jade Green). Ownership of the brand has changed twice: Yuga Labs acquired PROOF (Moonbirds, Oddities, Grails) on February 16, 2024, then sold the Moonbirds IP — together with Oddities and Mythics — to web3 gaming startup Orange Cap Games in a deal announced May 30, 2025.

## Cultural significance

Moonbirds was the defining launch of the late-cycle 2022 NFT market: roughly $280M in volume in its first two days made it briefly the top-trading collection, flipping BAYC and MAYC, and its "nesting" mechanic popularized soft-staking for PFP projects. Its cultural arc also tracks the market's turbulence — COO Ryan Carson quit nine days after launch to start an NFT fund (taking ~$1M in Moonbirds with him), drawing community backlash; the August 2022 switch to CC0 divided holders who felt exclusive image rights had been removed unilaterally; and the a16z-led $50M raise the same month made PROOF one of the best-capitalized NFT startups. The most famous single purchase was corporate rather than celebrity: metaverse firm The Sandbox bought Moonbird #2642 for 350 ETH (~$1M). Governance experiments included the Lunar Society DAO (February 2023, seeded with $2M from PROOF's treasury). After the market downturn, Yuga Labs absorbed PROOF and Moonbirds in February 2024, then sold the IP to Orange Cap Games in May 2025 — a hand-off that reportedly triggered a sharp floor-price rally and repositioned the owls toward gaming.

- **Enlightened (body, with Enlightened Purple background)** (6) — Grail-tier variant; carries exclusive legendary eye/eyewear/headwear attributes.

# Mutant Ape Yacht Club

## Overview

Mutant Ape Yacht Club (MAYC) is an Ethereum NFT collection of up to 20,000 "mutant" apes created by Yuga Labs as the first direct expansion of the Bored Ape Yacht Club (BAYC). It launched on August 28, 2021 in two halves: 10,000 Mutant Apes were sold to the public in a surprise Dutch auction that began at 3 ETH (~$10,000) and sold out in under an hour, grossing about $96 million; the other 10,000 could only be created by existing BAYC holders, who were airdropped 10,000 "Mutant Serum" vials (7,500 M1, 2,492 M2, and 8 M3 "Mega Mutant" serums). Applying a serum to a Bored Ape burns the serum and mints a new Mutant Ape — M1 and M2 mutants are warped versions that retain the original ape's traits, while the eight M3 serums produce entirely new one-of-a-kind "Mega Mutants."

The collection was framed by Yuga Labs as a way to bring newcomers into the BAYC membership ecosystem at a lower price point while rewarding existing holders with a free, sellable asset, and it had been on the BAYC roadmap since the original 2021 launch. As of mid-2026 roughly 19,566 of the maximum 20,000 mutants have been minted (some serums remain unused), held by about 12,000 addresses. MAYC holders received full ecosystem benefits, including 2,042 ApeCoin (APE) per mutant in the March 2022 airdrop (versus 10,094 per Bored Ape).

MAYC became one of the highest-volume NFT collections of the 2021–22 cycle, with its floor price peaking around 40 ETH (~$116,000) in April–May 2022 before falling more than 95% in the subsequent market decline. Its serum/mutation mechanic — burning a derivative token against an existing NFT to mint a new one — was widely imitated and is regarded as a landmark in NFT "expansion collection" design.

## Cultural significance

MAYC's launch was itself a cultural event: $96 million raised in under an hour made it one of the largest NFT drops to that point, and the serum airdrop pioneered the now-standard pattern of rewarding holders with a burnable derivative that mints a new asset. The collection functioned as the "second tier" of the most influential NFT membership brand of the era — MAYC holders received the March 2022 ApeCoin airdrop (2,042 APE each) and were included in subsequent Yuga ecosystem benefits — and its floor briefly reached ~40 ETH (~$116,000) at the April–May 2022 peak. Reported celebrity holders include Snoop Dogg (who assembled a full BAYC/MAYC set including M1 and M2 mutants), Shaquille O'Neal, and Lil Baby, and the theatrical Twitter Spaces "reveal parties" for multi-million-dollar Mega Mutant serum burns (notably Mega Trippy in February 2022) became emblematic of the 2021–22 NFT bull market. Like the wider market, MAYC later fell more than 95% from its price peak, but it remains among the highest all-time-volume NFT collections and a fixture of BAYC-ecosystem lore.

## Traits

|---|--:|
| Background | 17 |
| Fur | 39 |
| Eyes | 47 |
| Mouth | 67 |
| Clothes | 87 |
| Hat | 73 |
| Earring | 13 |
| Name | 12 |
| Trait | 5 |

**Famous rare traits:**

- **Mega Mutant (M3)** (13) — The collection's grail tier: 8 created by burning the 8 airdropped M3 Mega Mutant serums (token IDs 30000+) plus 5 included in the 10,000-item public mint. Each Mega is a fully unique design carrying a 'Name' trait rather than standard trait combinations.
- **Mega Trippy (MAYC #30005)** (1) — Created 2022-02 by applying an M3 serum (bought for 999 ETH, ~$3.8M) to BAYC #5235; holds the all-time MAYC sale record (2,300 ETH, Aug 2022).
- **Mega Demon (MAYC #4849)** (1) — Public-mint Mega; first headline MAYC sale at 350 ETH one day after launch.
- **M2 mutants** (max 2,492) — Only 2,492 M2 serums were airdropped, so M2-trait mutants are the rare mid-tier above the up-to-7,500 M1 mutants; individual M2 trait variants routinely fall under 1% of the collection.
- **Earring: None** (~70% of collection) — Earrings are the most skewed category — the 12 actual earring values are split across only ~30% of mutants.

# NodeMonkes

## Overview

NodeMonkes is a collection of 10,000 pixel-art monkey avatars inscribed directly onto individual satoshis on the Bitcoin blockchain via the Ordinals protocol. The artwork was inscribed in February 2023, only weeks after Casey Rodarmor launched Ordinals, giving the collection inscription numbers #83,522–#111,319 — roughly half the supply sits in the coveted sub-100k inscription range. It is widely described as the first original (non-derivative) 10k profile-picture collection fully inscribed on Bitcoin, a primacy claim contested by Bitcoin Frogs but generally conceded to NodeMonkes on the basis of its earlier inscription dates. Each monke carries traits drawn from four categories (Body, Head, Eyes, Earring); per the official Monkedex, 3,750 monkes have one trait, 2,147 have two, 499 have three, and only 13 carry four.

Although inscribed in early 2023, the collection was withheld from sale for most of that year. The anonymous two-person team — which published no roadmap and took no venture funding — sold 8,000 NodeMonkes in a descending Dutch auction on Magic Eden beginning December 21, 2023: the price opened at 0.21 BTC and dropped 0.005 BTC every six blocks (~hourly) until 8,000 valid bids set a clearing price of about 0.03 BTC (~$1,260). The collection surpassed 500 BTC in trading volume within four days of launch.

NodeMonkes became the flagship PFP of the Ordinals movement during the February–March 2024 Bitcoin rally: weekly secondary volume reached roughly $45 million, cumulative Magic Eden volume hit 2,795 BTC (~$190M) by early March 2024, the floor touched 0.81 BTC (~$52,000, up ~2,600% from mint), and on March 4, 2024 the "Alien Hoodie" NodeMonke #2769 sold for 17 BTC ($1.08M) — the first million-dollar NodeMonkes sale and, at the time, the second-highest Ordinals sale ever. In mid-March 2024 a 53% single-day floor surge briefly pushed the collection's market capitalization to ~$558.9 million, flipping Bored Ape Yacht Club.

## Cultural significance

NodeMonkes is routinely framed as "the CryptoPunks of Bitcoin": an anonymous-team, no-roadmap 10k pixel collection whose value case rests on provenance (sub-100k inscription numbers from February 2023) rather than promises. Its community slogan "Send Nodes" became one of the defining memes of the Ordinals movement. The collection anchored the early-2024 Bitcoin NFT boom — leading all NFT collections on any chain in weekly volume in early March 2024 — and on March 18, 2024 its market cap (~$558.9M after a 53% one-day floor surge) briefly flipped Bored Ape Yacht Club, a symbolic passing-of-the-torch moment for Bitcoin-native collectibles. It has remained the bellwether of the Bitcoin NFT market since: The Block (Oct 2025) noted NodeMonkes volume spikes cluster around Bitcoin all-time highs ($2.99M weekly volume in the October 2025 ATH week) and characterized the collection as a late-cycle sentiment gauge. No celebrity ownership is reliably documented.

## Traits

| Body | 32 |
| Head | 45 |
| Eyes | 29 |
| Earring | 5 |

**Famous rare traits:**

- **Alienate (Head)** (30) — Rarest trait in the collection per the official Monkedex; an alien-head homage to CryptoPunks' 9 Aliens, and the trait class behind the top sales.
- **Alien (Body)** (41) — The collection's grail body type; four Alien-body monkes sold for ~2 BTC each on Jan 3, 2024, and Alien Hoodie #2769 set the 17 BTC collection record in March 2024.
- **Cross (Earring)** (50) — Rarest of the five earring values (vs. Diamond 144, Gold 409, Silver 798).
- **Alienate (Eyes)** (55) — Rarest of the 29 eye values (next: Phase 109, Laser 149).
- **Gold (Body)** (102) — Second-scarcest body after Alien (Wrapped is third at 127).
- **Zombie (Body)** (217) — CryptoPunks Zombie homage; commands a premium over the ~500-count common bodies (e.g. Brown 558, Grey 557).

# Pudgy Penguins

## Overview

Pudgy Penguins is a collection of 8,888 profile-picture (PFP) NFTs on the Ethereum blockchain, each depicting a cartoon penguin assembled from roughly 150 hand-drawn traits. The collection minted on July 22, 2021 at 0.03 ETH (about $90) and sold out in under 20 minutes. It gained early mainstream attention when New York Times columnist Kevin Roose featured the project in an August 2021 column ("I Joined a Penguin NFT Club Because Apparently That's What We Do Now"), one of the first major-press treatments of "community NFT" culture.

The project was founded by a group of university students led by Cole Villemain (ColeThereum), with co-founder Clayton Patterson ("tubbyfat") and two pseudonymous collaborators. In January 2022 the community voted on Discord to oust Villemain and Patterson amid accusations of unmet roadmap promises and treasury mismanagement. In April 2022 Los Angeles entrepreneur Luca Netz (legal name Luca Schnetzler) acquired the project and its IP for 750 ETH (~$2.5 million) and refocused it as a consumer brand; the collection is operated by Igloo Inc.

Under Netz, Pudgy Penguins became the most prominent example of an NFT project crossing into mainstream retail: a physical toy line (Pudgy Toys, launched May 2023 with PMI) entered over 2,000 Walmart stores and later Target, Walgreens and Amazon, selling more than a million units and over $10 million in revenue in roughly its first year, with each toy unlocking a digital "Pudgy World" experience. In December 2024 the brand launched the PENGU token on Solana (88.88 billion supply, with ~25.9% airdropped to the community), and its parent company built Abstract, a consumer-focused Ethereum layer-2 network launched in January 2025. The ecosystem also includes Lil Pudgys (22,222 companion NFTs, December 2021) and Pudgy Rods.

## Cultural significance

Pudgy Penguins is widely cited as the NFT project that most successfully escaped the 2022 crypto downturn by becoming a mainstream IP brand. After the August 2021 New York Times column and a February 2022 Sotheby's auction ("Snowed In: A Rare Pudgy Penguins Sale", 10 NFTs for ~$129,000 total), the Netz era turned the penguins into a licensed consumer product: Walmart shelf space in 2,000+ stores (later 3,000+ plus Target, Walgreens, Amazon and Chuck E. Cheese), over a million toys sold, and official GIF stickers with tens of billions of GIPHY views (reports range from ~28.9B to 39B+), making the penguins a default reaction meme far beyond crypto. The December 2024 PENGU airdrop pushed the NFT floor above $100,000 (a 26.55 ETH / ~$101K sale), briefly pricing one penguin above one Bitcoin. Documented notable holders include Mark Cuban (sold his for over $30,000 in 2025 per The Block) and rapper Tory Lanez (bought in 2022); the January 2022 founder-ouster-by-Discord-vote and subsequent $2.5M community-driven sale remain a frequently referenced case study in NFT project governance.

## Traits

| Trait category | Distinct values |
|---|--:|
| Background | ? |
| Skin | ? |
| Body | ? |
| Face | ? |
| Head | ? |

**Famous rare traits:**

- **Green Background** (1) — Unique to Pudgy Penguin #6873 — the only green-background penguin in the collection (0.01%).
- **Black Skin** (1) — Unique to #6873 (0.01%).
- **Mirrored Body (left-facing)** (1) — #6873 is the only penguin in the 8,888 that faces left; this single trait drove its record sales.
- **Trick Or Treating Background** (~1 (0.01%)) — Carried by #5678, the second-rarest penguin, which has four one-of-a-kind traits.
- **Pillow Case Body** (~1 (0.01%)) — Also on #5678 (0.01% per Rarity Sniper).
- **Four-trait penguins** (~249 (2.8%)) — Only 2.8% of the collection has just 4 traits; the other 97.2% have 5 — fewer traits reads as rarer.

fm.contract: No smart contract -- Ordinals inscriptions on Bitcoin using the project's 'Evolving Inscriptions' architecture: each cat is a ~109-byte inscription referencing a shared Dispatcher inscription (rendering logic) plus Layer Connector inscriptions that map cat IDs to artwork assets across 40 art layers; artwork (~10MB total, spanning ~10 blocks) was inscribed in advance encrypted per-layer, with presigned transactions whose broadcast reveals decryption keys, so the art evolves in predetermined, pre-committed stages over time

# Quantum Cats

## Overview

Quantum Cats is a collection of 3,333 Ordinals inscriptions on Bitcoin created by Taproot Wizards, the Bitcoin-native NFT venture co-founded by Udi Wertheimer and Eric Wall, with artwork led by artist and engineer Francisco "FAR" Alarcon. Announced on January 12, 2024, the collection was conceived explicitly as a marketing and funding campaign to revive OP_CAT, a Bitcoin script opcode (short for "concatenate") present in Satoshi Nakamoto's original code but disabled in 2010, whose reactivation proponents argue would enable covenants, smart contracts, and bridges on Bitcoin. The cat imagery is a deliberate play on both the opcode's name and Schrodinger's cat: the official site frames the cats as existing in a "quantum realm," and the artwork itself changes state over time.

The collection's signature technology is "Evolving Inscriptions," billed as the first Ordinals collection whose art evolves on-chain. Multiple future versions of each cat were inscribed ahead of time in encrypted form (roughly 10MB of on-chain data spanning about 10 Bitcoin blocks, at an inscription cost reported around $66,000), with evolutions committed in advance so they unfold in predetermined ways as the OP_CAT proposal process advances. Per a technical write-up by Taproot Wizards CTO "Rijndael" in Bitcoin Magazine, each cat is a tiny (~109-byte) inscription that references a shared "Dispatcher" inscription for rendering logic, which in turn reads "Layer Connector" inscriptions mapping each cat to artwork assets across 40 art layers (backgrounds, body, eyes, mouth, etc.); artwork is encrypted per-layer and decryption keys are only revealed when presigned Layer Connector transactions are broadcast, hiding future traits and rarity until reveal.

The launch was one of the most-watched -- and most chaotic -- events of the early Ordinals era. The one-of-one "Genesis Cat" by FAR sold first, fetching 6.31 BTC (about $254,000, roughly 12x the high estimate) in Sotheby's "Natively Digital" curated Ordinals auction that closed January 22, 2024. The main sale of about 3,000 cats at a fixed 0.1 BTC (~$4,265) each began January 29, 2024, but was halted mid-sale by severe technical failures and postponed three times before completing on February 5, 2024, when the collection sold out for roughly $13 million -- most units going to whitelisted buyers in a five-hour exclusive window, with 313 cats selling in the first two seconds of the public phase. Within a day, the floor price on Magic Eden had more than doubled to 0.243 BTC.

Taproot Wizards had raised $7.5 million in seed funding in November 2023 (led by Standard Crypto, with StarkWare, UTXO Management, Bitcoin Frontier Fund and others) ahead of the drop. The campaign's political goal saw a milestone in April 2024 when the OP_CAT reactivation proposal received an official Bitcoin Improvement Proposal number, BIP-347 -- after the community, egged on by the Quantum Cats project, had tried to meme it into existence as "BIP-420." As of the most recent verified reporting, OP_CAT remains a proposal under debate rather than an activated Bitcoin upgrade.

## Cultural significance

Quantum Cats sits at the center of the 2023-2024 Ordinals movement that brought NFT-style collectibles -- and a bitter culture war -- to Bitcoin. Wertheimer and Wall, already famous as provocateurs for the original Taproot Wizards inscriptions, positioned the collection as more than art: it was an activism vehicle, using collectible sales to bankroll and popularize a soft-fork lobbying effort (OP_CAT / "BIP-420") -- a novel model where a meme collection doubles as protocol politics. The Sotheby's sale of the Genesis Cat at 12x its estimate was widely covered as a legitimization moment for Bitcoin-native digital art.

The mint itself became part of the lore: three public delays and a halted sale made headlines as an "embarrassment," yet the collection still sold out for ~$13M and immediately traded at multiples of mint, dominating Ordinals secondary volume in the following days. The "Evolving Inscriptions" mechanism -- encrypted, pre-committed art that changes as the OP_CAT campaign progresses -- is also cited as a genuine technical contribution to on-chain art on Bitcoin.

# Tensorians

## Overview

Tensorians is a 10,000-item profile-picture (PFP) NFT collection on Solana, created by the NFT marketplace Tensor as its native community collection ("A long time ago in a Solaxy far, far away..."). It minted on August 7-8, 2023 via a shard mechanic tied to Tensor's loyalty program: whitelist winners were airdropped Tensorian Shards (earned through Season 2 reward loot boxes, in four colors), and 10 shards of the same type plus 1.69 SOL (~$40 at the time) minted one Tensorian. The collection was designed to identify Tensor's "superfans": holding and staking Tensorians unlocked a gated Discord, reward-points multipliers (1.10x-1.50x depending on how many were staked), and targeted rewards. CoinMarketCap and community analysts describe it as the first 10k PFP collection launched as compressed NFTs (cNFTs), a Solana state-compression technology Tensor was first to support for trading.

The collection's market history tracks Tensor's own rise. As Tensor overtook Magic Eden to hold roughly 60% of Solana NFT trading volume in late 2023, Tensorians repriced from a ~$40 mint to a floor-price all-time high of 129 SOL (~$12,098) on January 4, 2024 per CoinGecko, with CoinMarketCap citing individual Tensorians changing hands above $11,400 in December 2023 — at peak it ranked among the largest Solana collections by market cap. The collection anchored the TNSR token launch: on April 8, 2024, 12.5% of the 1-billion TNSR supply (an airdrop valued around $250M) went to reward-box holders and Tensorian holders. The floor fell from ~28 SOL to 18 SOL (~$3,200) on airdrop day as holders realized profits, beginning a long decline; by mid-2026 the floor sat in the low single digits of SOL.

Structurally, marketplaces index 10,004 assets, including 14 guest-artist one-of-ones appended with IDs above #10000 (the #1-ranked "The Barbenheimer" among them). Each standard Tensorian is a robot/android rendered from up to 10 visual trait categories, and every revealed Tensorian belongs to one of four factions — Raider (2,234), Reaper (2,225), Mage (2,209), Android (2,201) — while 1,135 Tensorians remain permanently "Unrevealed," carrying only the tongue-in-cheek trait "Known for: Shipping It."

## Cultural significance

Tensorians is the flagship marketplace-native PFP of Solana's 2023-24 NFT resurgence: it was minted through loyalty-program shards rather than an open sale, functioned as a superfan membership pass (gated Discord, staking multipliers on Tensor reward points), and is widely cited as the first 10,000-piece PFP collection launched as compressed NFTs. Its fortunes mirrored Tensor's own — the marketplace, founded by Ilja Moisejevs and Richard Wu, seized roughly 60% of Solana NFT volume from Magic Eden in late 2023, and at peak Tensorians was described as the second-largest Solana collection by market cap behind Mad Lads. The collection became the centerpiece of one of "Airdrop April" 2024's biggest events, when 12.5% of the TNSR token supply (~$250M at launch) was airdropped to box holders and Tensorian holders on April 8, 2024; the same event triggered a sell-the-news crash to an 18 SOL floor and community friction over whether staked holders were rewarded fairly relative to casual participants. Its later slide to single-digit-SOL floors by 2026, after Tensor's team pivoted focus toward the Vector trading app, made Tensorians a frequently cited case study in the risks of platform-tied, airdrop-driven NFT valuations. No celebrity ownership is documented.

# VeeFriends

## Overview

VeeFriends is an Ethereum NFT project created by entrepreneur Gary Vaynerchuk ("GaryVee"), minted on May 11, 2021. The original collection (Series 1) comprises 10,255 ERC-721 tokens depicting 268 characters hand-drawn by Vaynerchuk — animals personifying traits he admires (Empathy Elephant, Patient Panda, "Diamond Hands" Hen). Tokens were sold through a roughly three-week Dutch auction (admission tokens settling around 0.5–3 ETH; access tokens listed as high as 49 ETH) and sold out by June 1, 2021; Vaynerchuk retained 1,242 tokens, later badged "GOO" (Gary's Original Ownership). Reported launch proceeds exceeded $20 million.

The project's defining pitch was utility over art: every Series 1 token doubled as a three-year ticket (2022–2024) to VeeCon, Vaynerchuk's annual conference, and the supply was split into three functional tiers — 9,400 Admission tokens (235 characters x 40 editions), 300 Access tokens redeemable for experiences with Vaynerchuk (32 characters: 165 group, 108 one-on-one, 22 competition, 5 scholarship), and 555 Gift Goat tokens carrying recurring physical gifts. This structure made VeeFriends one of the most-cited early examples of "utility NFTs."

Series 2 followed in April 2022 on a separate contract: 55,555 generative tokens across 251 characters (236 returning plus 15 new), each rendered in one of 8 poses against one of 74 scenes, minted at 0.335 ETH (about $995 at the time), with allocation mechanics tied to the Book Games burn token from Vaynerchuk's book "Twelve and a Half." The brand has since pushed heavily into physical licensing — Christie's-auctioned original drawings, Macy's and Toys "R" Us collectible lines (2022), zerocool/Topps trading cards, and Squishmallows and Mattel Creations collaborations (2025).

## Cultural significance

VeeFriends is the flagship of the "utility NFT" thesis and the vehicle for VeeCon, billed as the first NFT-ticketed super conference: the inaugural edition at U.S. Bank Stadium, Minneapolis (May 19–22, 2022) was open only to the 10,255 Series 1 token holders and featured Beeple, Deepak Chopra, Randi Zuckerberg, Logan Paul, Eva Longoria and Pharrell Williams, with Snoop Dogg, Spike Lee and Mila Kunis among attendees; later editions ran in Indianapolis (2023, ~5,000 attendees) and Los Angeles (2024), with no 2025 edition held. At Christie's in October 2021 five of Vaynerchuk's physical source drawings brought $1.26M — coverage noted the lots outsold Warhol and Pollock works in the same auction — and secondary NFT volume was reported above $90M within the first five months. The project's Discord was described as the largest NFT community server (~341k members, April 2022). VeeFriends has since become a licensing brand: Macy's and Toys "R" Us collectible figures (2022), zerocool/Topps trading cards, and 2025 Squishmallows and Mattel Creations collaborations.

- **Gift Goat (Series 1)** (555) — The single 'Gift' character; holders received a minimum of six physical gifts per year for three years plus VeeCon access
- **Access tokens (Series 1)** (300) — 32 characters granting experiences with Vaynerchuk: 165 group, 108 one-on-one (e.g. Dinner Deer, FaceTime Frog, Hangout Hawk), 22 competition, 5 scholarship
- **GOO badge (Gary's Original Ownership)** (1,242) — Tokens retained by Vaynerchuk at mint; GOO provenance drove the record Empathy Elephant sale

# World of Women

## Overview

World of Women (WoW) is a collection of 10,000 generative profile-picture NFTs (ERC-721) on Ethereum, launched on July 27, 2021 at a mint price of 0.07 ETH and sold out within its first day. Every layer was hand-drawn by artist Yam Karkai — roughly 200 individual drawings made over about two months, randomly combined into portraits of diverse women — with artwork hosted on IPFS. The project's stated purpose was to counter the near-total absence of women in early NFT/PFP culture and to fund female artists through the WoW Fund and later the WoW Foundation.

The founding team is Yam Karkai (artist and public face; a former acting student in Paris with a background in illustration, scriptwriting and translation) together with co-founders Raphaël Malavieille (project management; Karkai's partner), Toomaie (generative-art developer) and the pseudonymous BBA. Karkai deliberately designed a rounded "base woman" who could read as multiple ethnicities, named the 14 skin tones respectfully (an approach inspired by Fenty Beauty's shade range), and excluded imagery with religious or appropriation risk from the generative layers.

WoW became the defining female-led "blue chip" of the 2021–22 NFT cycle: it was signed by Guy Oseary (manager of Madonna, U2 and BAYC) for mainstream representation, struck a film/TV development deal with Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine (February 17, 2022), received a $25M five-year commitment from The Sandbox to create the WoW Foundation (announced February–March 2022), and made auction history at Christie's London in March 2022. A companion collection, World of Women Galaxy (22,222 NFTs, including 16 hand-drawn 1/1 "Champions and Guardians"), launched March 26, 2022 and generated roughly $79M in a day.

## Cultural significance

World of Women is widely credited as the first female-created NFT collection to reach blue-chip status, and it became the emblem of the push for representation in a space then dominated by male-coded PFPs. Early boosts came from Gary Vaynerchuk (whose Instagram endorsement drove a wave of buying) and collectors including Logan Paul and Steve Aoki; celebrity holders and supporters came to include Reese Witherspoon, Eva Longoria and Shonda Rhimes. In January–March 2022 the project stacked mainstream milestones in quick succession: representation by Guy Oseary, the Hello Sunshine partnership to adapt WoW characters into film and TV (announced February 17, 2022), The Sandbox's $25M WoW Foundation grant funding 3D avatars, a WoW Museum and Web3 education for women, features tied to Billboard's Women in Music, and the record Christie's London sale. The WoW Galaxy expansion ($79M in first-day sales, March 2022) and partnerships with brands from FC Barcelona and Mastercard to Sephora and Jazwares extended the IP beyond crypto; like most 2021-era PFPs, market prices later fell far from their 2022 peaks, but WoW remains the reference case for women-led NFT projects.

| Skin Tone | 14 |
| Hairstyle | 25 |
| Facial Features | 23 |
| Eyes | 28 |
| Background | 11 |

| Lips Color | 7 |

**Famous rare traits:**

- **Heterochromia Straight (Eyes)** (77) — Rarest reported trait value in the collection — two different-colored eyes, straight gaze (0.77%).
- **Resting Butterfly (Face Accessories)** (83) — A butterfly resting on the face; among the scarcest accessory values.
- **Night Goddess (Skin Tone)** (85) — Rarest of the 14 skin tones (0.85%); the marquee 'grail' skin comparable to CryptoPunks' Alien tier within WoW.
- **Heterochromia Eye Roll (Eyes)** (85) — Second heterochromia variant, eyes rolled upward.
- **Red Blue Bolt (Facial Features)** (97) — Lightning-bolt face marking in red/blue; rarest facial-feature value reported.
- **Naiade (Clothes)** (98) — Rarest clothing value reported by rarity trackers.

Live data on the [Market page](../../app/market.html) (cross-platform tab). As of 2026-08-03: floor **$220**, marketcap **$2,202,427** (floor-based), 5,281 holders.

# VeVe Collect Wiki

A public, iterative **fandom taxonomy** for **VeVe / Collect Chain (Stackr)** — officially licensed digital collectibles.

## The Taxonomy (4 layers)

| Layer | `type` | Folder | Example |
|-------|--------|--------|---------|
| Universe / IP world | `domain` | `wiki/domains/` | [[marvel\|Marvel]] |
| Fandom / character / brand | `entity` | `wiki/entities/` | [[spider-man\|Spider-Man]] |
| Collection (a series/drop — 15-axis taxonomy + first-appearances) | `collection` | `wiki/collections/` | _(per series)_ |
| One VeVe collectible (NFT) | `collectible` | `wiki/collectibles/` | _(per item)_ |

Entities link **up** to their universe; collectibles link **up** to their collection (inheriting its fandom/era/franchise). Full rules in [[conventions]] and the vault `CLAUDE.md`.

## How It's Built

This is an **iterative** wiki — **coverage first, depth later**. The skeleton fills only confident facts; everything else is `# TODO`. **No invented licensors, dates, or URLs.** Rights-holders in flux carry a `> [!warning] Licensor flag`.

## Start Here

- All universes → [[domains/_index|Domains Index]]
- All fandoms/brands → [[entities/_index|Entities Index]]
- The rest of the 200+ catalog → [[_catalog-backlog|Catalog Backlog]]
- How VeVe works → [[platform/platform|Platform reference]]
- Terms → [[glossary]]

## Status (2026-06-26)

Built on the owner's **authoritative Collect Chain data export**: **49 domains · 822 entities · 1,865 taxonomy collections · 2,481 collectibles** (real editions + **VeVe market floors**) · **~3,819 comic issues** · 391 sets · ~5,270 pages, **0 dead links**. The three live app tools price by real VeVe floor (💠) → StackR on-chain (⛓) → drop price. Remaining: depth (lore / notable-mints) on the newest collectibles — see [[hot]] + [[log]].

platform/blind-boxes.md:
# Blind Boxes — Mystery Drops

A **blind box** is a VeVe drop where a whole series is released at once and the buyer is assigned a *random* member of it — item, rarity and edition number all unknown until the collectible is delivered. It is the platform's dominant release format: **1,539 of the 2,849 collectibles** in this wiki's catalog (54%) belong to a blind-box series, spread across **359 series** and every season from 2 to 11 (earliest recorded blind drop **2021-08-14**, most recent in our data **2026-04-19**). The format also carries a pricing trap that this page exists to spell out: **one sealed-box price covers members whose real values differ by a median 9×**, so a blind item's list price tells you almost nothing about what that item is worth. See [[Blind Box]] for the concept-level definition.

## How a blind box drop works

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| Release | Multiple collectibles from one series drop simultaneously. VeVe's storefront labels the drop type **"Blindbox"** or **"Blindbox & Waitlist"**. |
| Entry | Waitlist opens 12h before and closes 5 min before the drop. Allocation is **not** purely random: **40% of reservations are allocated by MCP Priority Bidding** (highest bidders win), with a **5,000 minimum Points bid** on blind boxes; the rest is randomly allocated with priority to KYC-verified collectors (see [[Drop Types]]). Timings come from VeVe's 101 waitlist article, which is partly superseded — its 5-minute purchase window is stated as 7 minutes on 2024–25 drop pages. |
| Price | You pay **one list price in Gems** for the box, not a per-item price (1 Gem = 1 USD). |
| Assignment | You receive a random member of the series. Per VeVe: *"the rarity and edition numbers are also randomly allocated and will not be known to you until you have completed the purchase and the collectible has been delivered."* |
| Delivery | The revealed collectible lands in the wallet. From that point it is an ordinary collectible — tradeable on VeVe's market and on StackR. |

Because the combined edition pool of a whole series is larger than any single item's, blind-box drops are generally **easier to win** than single-item drops — vevepedia notes this explicitly. It is also how VeVe seeds most of its chase material: **335 of the catalog's 682 Secret Rares** (49%) come out of blind-box series.

## Are the odds published?

Yes — and this is unusual enough to be worth stating plainly. A blind-box collectible's **public storefront page lists per-variant odds** in the form `Odds: 1 in X`, for the item and its series-mates, visible **before** purchase and without logging in (verified unauthenticated on all four storefront pages cited below; not confirmed catalog-wide). The odds live on the *storefront*, not in the announcement — VeVe's own drop posts for *Labyrinth* and *Diablo* publish edition sizes and price but no odds at all.

Verified example — *Creatures of Jim Henson's Labyrinth*, a 4-piece blind box at a **30 Gem** box price (fetched 2026-07-30):

| Variant | Rarity | Editions | Published odds |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| [[labyrinth-ludo\|Ludo]] | Common | 4,800 | 1 in 2.62 |
| [[labyrinth-hoggle\|Hoggle]] | Uncommon | 3,600 | 1 in 3.51 |
| [[labyrinth-goblin-knight\|Goblin Knight]] | Rare | 2,300 | 1 in 5.58 |
| [[labyrinth-sir-didymus\|Sir Didymus]] | Secret Rare | 1,986 | 1 in 6.48 |

### The odds are not simply "editions ÷ set total"

The published number tracks the **live pool**, not the total minted edition size — so it drifts as a drop sells, and items with nothing left to sell drop out of the odds display entirely. The [[collections/disney-stitch-unleashed-series|Disney Stitch Unleashed Series]] Secret Rare is the clean test case (box price **20 Gems**):

| Basis for the odds | Implied odds — [[disney-stitch-blaster-ready\|Blaster Ready]] (Secret Rare) |
|---|--:|
| **VeVe's published figure** | **1 in 7.83** |
| Share of total issued editions (626 / 4,676) | 1 in 7.47 |
| Share of circulating editions (576 / 4,526) | 1 in 7.86 |
| Share of still-available store editions (511 / 4,032) | 1 in 7.89 |

> [!warning] Unverified — the odds formula
> VeVe publishes the odds but **does not document how they are computed**, and no official explainer was found. Reconstructing them from the authoritative edition figures, the *live* pool (circulating / still-available) fits within ~1% while total-issued editions is off by 5%, which implies the displayed odds move during a drop. Treat the exact basis as inferred, not stated. Series that mix mechanics do **not** reconcile cleanly: in the *Sabretooth* series only the two Commons are blind-box pulls, the rest are drop type **Craft**, and no single denominator reproduces both published figures.

## There is no sealed box on VeVe

Physical blind-box collecting has a whole secondary market in **unopened** boxes, which trade at a premium precisely because the option is still alive. **VeVe has no equivalent.** The randomisation resolves at purchase; what enters the wallet — and therefore the only thing that can ever be listed on VeVe's market or on StackR — is the **revealed** collectible. There is no sealed-box asset to hold, gift, or flip, and nothing named or flagged as one exists anywhere in the 2,849-item catalog.

> [!warning] Unverified — absence of evidence
> VeVe does not publish a statement of the form "boxes cannot be held sealed." The conclusion above rests on the official reveal-on-delivery wording plus the absence of any sealed-box product in the authoritative catalog. If VeVe ever ships a holdable mystery box, this section is the part that breaks.

Practical consequence: **"sealed vs opened value" is not a VeVe concept.** The nearest real analogue is *expected value of a pull* — box price versus the odds-weighted value of the possible outcomes — which is a calculation, not a tradeable asset.

## The pricing caveat — a box price is not an item price

**338 of the 359 blind-box series** in the catalog carry one identical list price across every member, which is exactly what a single sealed-box price looks like in the data. The **21 exceptions** are not one phenomenon: some mix blind-box pulls with **Craft**-obtained items priced separately (verified against VeVe's own pages for *Sabretooth* — 20.00 for the pull vs 6.99/9.99 for the crafts), others carry several genuinely different prices (*Gambit* spans 10/15/20/30, *Human Torch* 40/50/60), and several contain members with no recorded price at all. Counting an unpriced member as a mismatch lowers the uniform count to 314. Median box price across blind items: **20 Gems** (the median of the 359 per-series prices is 25).

That single price then has to stand in for outcomes that are worth wildly different amounts — so quoting it as "the price" of any one member is wrong, and wrong in *both* directions.

### What blind pulls actually trade for

Measured on **real completed sales** (trailing monthly median traded price, as of 2026-07-29), across the 105 blind-box series where every member of a 3+ piece set has traded recently:

| Measure | Value |
|---|--:|
| Median spread between the best and worst member of a series | **9.3×** |
| Same, 25th / 75th percentile | 4.0× / 21.7× |
| Median: top member's traded price ÷ box price | **1.67×** |
| Median: bottom member's traded price ÷ box price | **0.17×** |
| Series with at least one member trading **below** the box price | 100 of 105 |
| Series with at least one member trading **above** the box price | 73 of 105 |

> [!warning] Unverified — the sale-mirror aggregates
> The six figures above are re-reported from the internal sale mirror and were **not** re-derived during fact-check. Two catalog aggregates on this page that *were* re-derived came back wrong (the uniform-price series count and the median box price, both corrected above), so treat these spread multiples as indicative of direction, not as settled numbers.

Worked example — [[collections/stanley-gibbons-the-penny-red|Stanley Gibbons – The Penny Red]], a **10 Gem** box:

| Variant | Rarity | Editions | Traded median | Sales/30d |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| [[stanley-gibbons-penny-red-nk\|Penny Red — NK]] | Secret Rare | 110 | **225.00** | 2 |
| [[stanley-gibbons-penny-red-aa-ef\|Penny Red — AA-EF]] | Ultra Rare | 1,841 | 15.50 | 2 |
| [[stanley-gibbons-penny-red-ig-jl\|Penny Red — IG-JL]] | Rare | 2,841 | 2.60 | 7 |
| [[stanley-gibbons-penny-red-ch-di\|Penny Red — CH-DI]] | Common | 3,841 | **0.90** | 66 |

A 10 Gem box that resolves, most of the time, into a collectible worth **0.90 Gems** — and occasionally into one worth 225. Neither number is "the list price," and the list price describes neither.

> [!note] House rule (applies to the app and this wiki)
> For any blind-box item: **never present a store count, an unsold count, or the drop/list price as a value.** Show a **real secondary floor** (VeVe Gems 💠 or StackR OMI ⛓) or show nothing. This is a standing correction, not a preference. Note also that a "floor" is a *lowest ask*, not a trade — see [[platform/floor-prices]]; the traded medians above are used here precisely because asks on illiquid blind-box variants are unreliable.

## Rarity tier is not the same as the chase

Two independent effects break the intuition that a higher [[Rarity and Editions|rarity tier]] means a better pull:

**1. The chase can sit inside a rarity tier.** In the *Sabretooth* blind box both pulls were **Common** — `Savage Presence` (6,860 editions, 1 in 1.55) and `Savage Presence Special Edition` (140 editions, 1 in 85.99). Same tier, ~55× difference in odds, and current asks of **8.80** vs **750** Gems.

**2. Traded prices do not order by tier.** [[collections/lamborghini-diablo|Lamborghini Diablo]], a **70 Gem** box, has its Ultra Rare trading *below* its Uncommon:

| Variant | Rarity | Editions | Traded median | Sales/30d |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| [[lamborghini-diablo-gold\|Diablo — Gold]] | Secret Rare | 640 | 99.00 | 3 |
| [[lamborghini-diablo-yellow\|Diablo — Yellow]] | Rare | 1,590 | 22.71 | 4 |
| [[lamborghini-diablo-purple\|Diablo — Purple]] | Uncommon | 1,990 | 12.45 | 3 |
| [[lamborghini-diablo-orange\|Diablo — Orange]] | Ultra Rare | 1,000 | 10.63 | 8 |

> [!warning] Thin markets
> Several of these medians rest on a handful of sales in the window (3–8, and 2 for the Penny Red top tiers). Direction is meaningful; the exact figure is not. Colourway and character desirability visibly compete with rarity, but a single month of thin trading cannot settle which dominates in general.

## How much of the catalog is blind

Every standard rarity tier runs **49–62%** blind-box in origin — the format is not reserved for chases:

| Rarity | Blind-box items | All catalog items | Share |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Common | 318 | 510 | 62% |
| Uncommon | 236 | 386 | 61% |
| Rare | 294 | 541 | 54% |
| Ultra Rare | 355 | 610 | 58% |
| Secret Rare | 335 | 682 | 49% |
| *No standard tier* | 1 | 120 | 1% |
| **Total** | **1,539** | **2,849** | **54%** |

The five tiers alone sum to 1,538 / 2,729; the remaining **120** catalog rows sit outside them — **111 Artist Proof**, **8** with rarity still `# TODO`, and **1** labelled `Common Special Edition` (*Buzz Lightyear – Galactic Glow*, the only blind item of the three groups).

Median blind-box series size is **4** members (range 2–12). Of the 1,539 blind items, **1,473** currently have some market floor recorded; 66 have never had one.

## Duplicates, set completion and MCP

Random assignment interacts badly with [[Master Collector Points]] in one direction and well in another:

- **Duplicates are penalised.** A second copy of the same collectible earns 0.75 points/day, a third 0.35, a fourth-or-later 0.10. Repeated pulls of the same common are close to worthless for rank.
- **Completion is rewarded.** Finishing a set pays a one-off **+100**, plus daily points scaled to set size — **5.0/day** only at 5+ members, **4.0/day** at 4, which is the median blind-box series size. A duplicate completed set earns 30% of set points, then 20%, then 10%.
- **MCP is also an input, not just a reward.** Entering a blind-box waitlist via Priority Bidding costs a **5,000-Point minimum bid**, and points are forfeited if you win a reservation and then don't buy. Spending points to win the box competes with holding items to earn them.

So the format's MCP value is front-loaded on breadth: the pulls that complete a set are worth far more than the pulls that repeat one. This is also why blind-box items are excluded from the app's optimiser whenever no real floor exists — without a genuine market price, points-per-Gem cannot be computed honestly.

## Data provenance — which field to trust

- **Authoritative flag:** `series.isBlindbox` in the Collect/VeVe data (surfaced as `blind` on each catalog row, 1,539 items). Blind-box status is a property of the **series**, not of the individual collectible.
- **Do not** use the `release: blind-box` axis on `wiki/collections/` pages as a source of truth: it is classifier-assigned, disagrees with the authoritative flag on 130 of 846 matched series, and is applied to 905 comic collections, which are not blind boxes at all.

## See also

- [[Blind Box]] · [[Drop Types]] · [[platform/drops|Drops]]
- [[platform/floor-prices]] (why a floor is an ask, not a trade) · [[platform/record-sales]]
- [[Secret Rare]] · [[Rarity and Editions]] · [[Significant Mints]]

# Collect Chain

**Collect Chain** is the blockchain every VeVe collectible now lives on — an EVM chain VeVe says it "helped create", replacing VeVe's previous home on Immutable X. VeVe announced it on 19 Nov 2025 and declared the migration complete on 1 Apr 2026. Ownership is publicly auditable through the chain's Blockscout explorer, **[collectscan.com](https://collectscan.com)** — but only ownership and metadata: prices, [[Gems]] balances, listings and identities all stay in VeVe's private database.

## The chain today

Live figures below were read from the collectscan public API on **2026-07-30**; they move constantly.

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Explorer | `https://collectscan.com` (Blockscout, backend `v9.0.2`) | live API |
| Public JSON-RPC | `https://collectscan.com/api/eth-rpc` (explorer proxy) | live probe |
| Chain ID | `201850817` (`0xc07ffc1`) | `eth_chainId` via the proxy |
| Token contracts on the chain | **1** — `VeVe` (`VEVE`), ERC-721 | `/api/v2/tokens` |
| Contract address | `0xbcFEbA7A9dA14f5C9453bDA72E2098537867B3c7` | live API |
| Holder addresses (VeVe contract) | 707,901 | `/tokens/{addr}/counters` |
| Total VeVe transfers | 14,117,798 | `/tokens/{addr}/counters` |
| Total chain addresses | 708,463 | `/api/v2/stats` |
| Total chain transactions | 1,582,458 | `/api/v2/stats` |
| Block height | 61,943,591 | `/api/v2/stats` |
| Reported average block time | 148 ms — **not representative**, see next row | `/api/v2/stats` |
| Measured block interval | **~250 ms**, steady over the last 100 / 10k / 100k blocks | `eth_getBlockByNumber` timestamp deltas |
| First timestamped block | block 1 = **2026-01-13 09:45 UTC** (block 0 carries timestamp 0) | `eth_getBlockByNumber` |
| Gas price | 1.01 (all tiers — slow/average/fast identical) | `/api/v2/stats` |
| Native coin price / market cap | `null` / `0` — no priced native asset exposed | `/api/v2/stats` |

The single most useful structural fact: **the entire chain is one ERC-721 contract.** Collectibles *and* comics are token IDs inside `0xbcFE…B3c7`. There is no separate comics contract, no ERC-1155, and no ERC-20 on the token list.

> [!warning] Unverified — operator, "Layer 2", launch date
> - **Who operates the chain is not published.** VeVe's 19 Nov 2025 post says only that "we helped create Collect"; `collect.app` names a team (CEO, CTO, engineers) but no company. Neither names **ECOMI**, and no filing or announcement attributing the chain to a legal entity was found. Operator: `# TODO`.
> - `collect.app` markets Collect as a **"Layer 2"** EVM chain with **100 ms block times**, but does not say what it settles to, and no bridge, sequencer or settlement contract is publicly documented. VeVe's own 19 Nov 2025 announcement calls it only "a blockchain purpose-built for digital collectibles" — it says nothing about L2 or EVM. Treat "L2" as marketing language until a settlement layer is documented; the "100 ms" is also off by ~2.5× against the measured ~250 ms interval.
> - Chain ID `201850817` does **not** appear in public chain registries — checked against `chainid.network/chains.json` (2,667 entries) on 2026-07-30, no match. It is attested only by the explorer's own RPC proxy.
> - **Chain age is measured, not inferred:** block 1 is timestamped **2026-01-13**, so this chain's history begins **January 2026** — the month VeVe put Phase 1 at, not `collect.app`'s "Chain Launch — Late 2025 — Completed". Either the launch predates this genesis (re-genesis) or "launch" means something other than block 0. Unresolved.

## Migration timeline

| When | What | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| 2020–2021 | VeVe collectibles on **GoChain** — migrated token ID 1 carries `dropDate: 2020-10-14`, so drops predate 2021 | medium — third-party accounts + on-chain metadata |
| **15 Dec 2021** | VeVe goes live on **Immutable X** (Ethereum L2, StarkEx); "2.6 million+ premium licensed NFTs", gasless trading | high — launch press release |
| **19 Nov 2025** | **"Introducing Collect"** — migration announced. Phase 1 (move the NFTs) stated to complete **January 2026**; Phase 2 = optional self-custody | high — official post |
| Dec 2025 | Collect website launched | medium — third-party summary |
| early 2026, writes blocked **from 11 Feb 2026** | **Immutable X merged into Immutable Chain**; legacy StarkEx rollup no longer processes new transactions | high — Immutable deprecation doc ("early 2026") + published write-block date |
| **1 Apr 2026** | **"VeVe Completes Full Migration on Collect Chain"** — Collect now underpins every VeVe collectible; new explorer introduced | high — official post |
| not yet shipped | **Phase 2 — optional self-custody** | high |

> [!warning] Date caveats — Phase 1 vs "complete", and the Immutable X wind-down
> - **Phase 1 slipped, or "complete" means two things.** The Nov 2025 announcement put the NFT migration at January 2026; the official completion post is dated 1 April 2026. VeVe has not published a reconciliation. Some third-party write-ups report Phase 1 as done in Jan 2026 and *full catalogue* migration in Apr 2026 — plausible, but not stated officially.
> - **Immutable X was staged down, not switched off on a day.** Immutable's deprecation doc dates the merge only to "early 2026"; its published schedule blocks all writes (POST) via Immutable X APIs/RPCs from **11 Feb 2026 at the earliest**, after which the rollup is read-only, with removal of deprecated interfaces unscheduled. There is no single "shutdown day" to cite.

`collect.app` states the **first wave** of migration moved **11 million NFTs and 660,000 accounts**. That is the right order of magnitude against the live chain: 707,901 holder addresses, and 12,607,493 of the 14.1M VeVe transfers involve the zero address — i.e. the overwhelming majority of all transfers on this chain are **mints**, consistent with a bulk re-mint of the back catalogue.

## What is verifiable on-chain

Everything here is readable by anyone, with no login, from `collectscan.com/api/v2/...` (CORS is open — see [[data-landscape-and-apis]] for the endpoint map).

- **Existence of every edition** — one token ID per minted copy.
- **Current owner address** of any edition.
- **Full transfer history** per edition, per address, and per contract.
- **Mints** — a transfer from `0x0000…0000`.
- **Burns** — would appear as a transfer *to* `0x0000…0000`. There is no evidence of a conventional burn sink: `0x…dEaD` has **zero** VeVe transfers.
- **Aggregate holder distribution** — addresses and balances, paginated.
- **Per-edition metadata**, embedded on each token instance:

| Metadata field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | collectible title |
| `brand` | brand / character grouping |
| `series` | the drop or series it belongs to |
| `licensor` | the rights-holder (e.g. `tokidoki`) |
| `rarity` | Common → Secret Rare (see [[Rarity and Editions]]) |
| `edition` | the mint number |
| `totalEditions` | the edition size |
| `editionType` | e.g. `FE` (First Edition) |
| `dropDate` / `mintDate` | the **original** VeVe drop/mint dates, preserved |
| `image`, `description` | asset + blurb |

Field presence varies by item type — comic tokens carry additional comic-specific keys. A representative live read: *Dragon Girl - Silver / Black*, Uncommon, edition 87 of 4,888, `licensor: tokidoki`, `dropDate: 2021-05-13`.

## What stays in VeVe's database

None of the following is on-chain, and none of it has an official public API. This is the real data gap for anyone building on Collect Chain.

| Off-chain | Notes |
|---|---|
| [[Gems]] balances and Gem-denominated store prices | closed-loop, 1 Gem = US$1 |
| Marketplace listings, asks and [[platform/floor-prices\|floor prices]] | a floor is a lowest *ask*, not a traded value |
| Completed sale prices | this project mirrors 300k+ real sales since 2025-07-12 across VeVe (Gems) and StackR (OMI) |
| Username ↔ wallet mapping | **private by design** — see [[identity-username-wallet]] |
| [[Master Collector Points]] | scoring, tiers, OMI reward tier |
| [[Blind Box]] contents before opening | the reveal is a server-side assignment |
| Lowest public mint / reserve counts | editions below the lowest public mint are held back by VeVe (often #1–40, varies per item) |
| Set definitions, taxonomy collections, season labels | ~2,850 collectibles, ~3,856 comic issues, 1,865 taxonomy collections in this wiki's catalogue |
| Store inventory / unsold counts | primary-sale state |

Note also that [[OMI Token|OMI]] and the StackR secondary market are **not on Collect Chain** — StackR runs on **Base** and settles in OMI. Two markets, two chains.

## Gotchas when reading the chain

Four traps that will silently corrupt any analysis built on collectscan:

1. **`mintDate` metadata is not the on-chain mint.** Metadata preserves the original VeVe dates (a 2021 collectible still reads `mintDate: 2021-05-13`), but the token itself was created during the 2026 migration. **On-chain history does not reach back before the migration** — pre-migration provenance from GoChain and Immutable X is not in this chain's transfer log.
2. **A "holder" is often the platform.** The top address holds **1,453,597** editions and the second **524,053** — roughly 2.0M editions between them. These are platform-scale balances (reserves, unsold store inventory), not collectors. Holder counts are not collector counts.
3. **Listing appears to move the token.** Roughly 1.21M transfers — about **80% of all non-mint VeVe transfers** — pass through a single high-throughput address that holds only ~38,800 editions at rest. The pattern (out on list, back on delist) is what a custodial marketplace escrow looks like, which means the on-chain owner of a *listed* item may be the platform rather than the collector. *(Inference from transfer shape, not confirmed by VeVe.)*
4. **`total_supply` is `null`** on the contract endpoint. Supply must be reconstructed by paginating `/instances`.

## Custody

Collectibles are **custodial today**. VeVe generates a wallet per account (email login, no seed phrase to manage), and a collector can read their own address in the VeVe wallet (Send/Receive OMI → Receive) — but cannot move a collectible out of the VeVe ecosystem. Optional self-custody is **Phase 2, announced and still not live** as of 2026-07-30. Until it ships, the exit path runs through VeVe and StackR, not through a personal wallet.

## Sources

- https://www.veve.me/blog/veve/updates/veve-completes-full-migration-on-collect-chain/
- https://www.collect.app/
- https://collectscan.com — live reads on 2026-07-30 of `/api/v2/stats`, `/api/v2/tokens`, `/api/v2/tokens/{addr}/counters`, `/api/v2/tokens/{addr}/holders`, `/api/v2/tokens/{addr}/transfers`, `/api/v2/tokens/{addr}/instances`, `/api/v2/config/backend-version`, `/api/v2/addresses/{addr}/counters`, and `eth_chainId` + `eth_blockNumber` + `eth_getBlockByNumber` via `/api/eth-rpc`

# Collectibles

The kinds of digital collectibles available on [[VeVe]].

## Types

- **Premium Collectibles** — high-detail 3D digital figures/sculptures. The flagship format. Viewable in AR and in your [[platform|showroom]].
- **Comics** — officially licensed digital comics, readable in the app's comic reader.
- **Digital Art** — 2D artwork pieces and posters.
- **Other formats** — stickers, cards, and other items appear from time to time. _(to verify current list)_

## What Makes Them Collectible

Every collectible is a **limited edition** with a unique **mint number** within its edition. See [[Rarity and Editions]]. Some drops hide an ultra-rare [[Secret Rare]] variant, and many are sold via randomized [[Blind Box]] mechanics.

platform/drops.md:
# Drops

How new collectibles are released. *(Platform reference.)*

## Drop vs Market
- **Drop** = timed primary release (Store).
- **Market** = secondary collector-to-collector resale (fixed price + auctions).

## Formats → [[Drop Types]]
- **Single-item** · **[[Blind Box]]** (random pull) · **Store** (incl. post-drop leftovers).

## Waitlist / Queue *(high)*
- Opens **12h before**, closes **5 min before** the drop.
- **Random allocation**, **KYC users prioritized**.
- Winners get a **5-minute** purchase window; missed reservations return to public allocation (~7 min after).
- No need to pre-load [[Gems]].

## Why it matters
Drops are the heartbeat of the platform and where [[Rarity and Editions|edition sizes & mint numbers]] (and [[Secret Rare]]s) are set — the upstream of everything the wiki and app track (floor history, holder distribution, set membership).

## Connections
- Formats → [[Drop Types]], [[Blind Box]]
- Produces → collectibles in [[platform/collectibles|collectibles]]
- Priced in → [[Gems]]

## Sources
- [[catalog-rarity-drops]]

# ECOMI

**ECOMI** is the company behind [[veve|VeVe]], **rebranding to "Collect"** (2025–26) alongside its own blockchain, **Collect Chain**. Founded 2018 in Auckland, New Zealand.

## Key facts
- **Product:** the [[veve|VeVe]] digital-collectibles app. *(high)*
- **Token:** [[OMI Token|OMI]] — external settlement asset; converts to [[Gems]] on **StackR** (a separate Base marketplace). *(high)*

platform/economy.md:
# Economy

How value flows through VeVe / Collect. *(Platform reference — supplementary to the fandom taxonomy.)*

## Currencies

- **[[Gems]]** — in-app currency, **1 Gem = US$1**; non-refundable, non-transferable, non-withdrawable (since 19 Nov 2025). Everything in-app is priced in Gems.
- **[[OMI Token]]** — external crypto asset. Funds Gems via **OMI→Gem on StackR** ($1 OMI = 1 Gem, 7% burn + 3% fee). Not used inside the app.

## The funding path

```
OMI (open market)  →  StackR (Base)  →  convert to Gems ($1=1, 7% burn +3% fee)  →  buy collectibles in VeVe
        └─ holding OMI also earns bonus daily MCP (OMI Reward Tier)
```

## What drives value

- **[[Rarity and Editions|Rarity & low mint]]** — scarcity premiums.
- **Demand** — brand/character popularity.
- **[[Secret Rare]] pulls** — the most valuable drop outcomes.
- **Floor price** — lowest active [[platform/marketplace|marketplace]] listing.

## Master Collector Points
The **[[Master Collector Points|MCP]]** program is a parallel "score economy" — points are earned by *holding* (not spending), so the economy rewards smart collection-building, not just spend. This is the basis of the app's MCP optimizer.

> [!warning] Volatile / corrections
> - Any specific prices, market caps, or token figures are time-sensitive — cite + timestamp.
> - **StackR is a separate marketplace (Base), not a rebrand of VeVe.** **Collect** = the company + chain.

## Sources
- [[economy-gems-omi-mcp]]

platform/floor-prices.md:
# Floor Prices — StackR & VeVe

How the web app sources a "floor" (lowest available price) for a collectible. There are **two distinct markets**, and they are NOT equally accessible. Strict accuracy policy applies: **we never fabricate a price — an unknown floor is shown as `—`, never estimated.**

## TL;DR

| Market | What it is | Accessible for free? | How we get it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **StackR** | Peer-to-peer secondary market, **on-chain on Base**, priced in OMI | ✅ Yes — public chain data | Index `StackrListings` events via Blockscout → `app/data/floor.js` |
| **VeVe — drop/list price** | The official **primary** price at the moment of the drop, in Gems (1 Gem = $1) | ✅ Yes — published | `drop_price_gems` in each collectible's frontmatter |
| **VeVe — live in-app market floor** | Lowest current ask in VeVe's **own** in-app secondary market | ❌ **No free/automated source** | Login-gated GraphQL — see options below |

## 1. StackR floor (on-chain, free, automated) — SOLVED

StackR is a secondary marketplace whose listings settle **on-chain on Base**, so every listing is public data — no login, no ToS issue.

- **Contract:** `StackrListings` — `0x5ccdcd1592cf055ae08e35f948f7627473c55432` (Base)
- **VeVe NFT contract:** `0xbcFEbA7A9dA14f5C9453bDA72E2098537867B3c7`
- **Method** (`/tmp/gen_floor.py` → `app/data/floor.js` = `window.FLOOR`):
  1. Page `ItemListed` events via the free Blockscout API (`base.blockscout.com/api/v2`).
  2. Reconcile **active** listings = `ItemListed` − (`ItemBought` ∪ `ItemCanceled` ∪ `ItemReleased`), keyed by `listingId`.
  3. Resolve each active listing's VeVe `tokenId` → collectible name via collectscan instance metadata.
  4. Convert OMI → USD using CoinGecko (`ecomi`), keep the **lowest** active OMI price per name.
- **Pay token:** OMI (`0x3792DBDD07e87413247DF995e692806aa13D3299`, 18 decimals).
- **Refresh model:** snapshot — re-run the indexer to refresh. For fuller, fresher coverage run it server-side / on a cron (Blockscout throttles one-off IPs, capping a single local run — a 150-page run times out).
- **In the app (already wired):** the optimizer and Set Tracker render this one on-chain floor as **💎 Gems** — because OMI→USD is converted, and at **1 Gem = $1** the USD figure *is* the Gem figure. So a single free on-chain source yields **OMI, USD, and Gem** values at once. (`app/mcp.html` `costOf()`, `app/sets.html`.)
- **Caveat:** StackR carries only items people have *chosen* to list there; many collectibles have **no StackR listing**, so they have no StackR floor (shown as `—`). It is a *secondary* market signal, not VeVe's primary price.

## 2. VeVe drop / list price (primary, free) — HAVE IT

Every drop has an official **list price in Gems** (1 Gem = $1), published on `veve.me/blog/collectibles/<slug>`. This is captured per item as `drop_price_gems`. It is the **primary** price (what VeVe first sold it for), **not** a live floor — values move after the drop. The app uses it as the honest VeVe-side reference when no live market floor is available.

## 3. VeVe live in-app market floor — NO FREE AUTOMATED SOURCE (verified 2026-06-26)

VeVe's in-app secondary market (buy the cheapest existing copy on VeVe itself) is the price most people *mean* by "the VeVe floor." It is **not freely obtainable** by an automated, ToS-respecting method. Evidence gathered:

- **VeVe's own public/logged-out storefront** (`veve.me/collectibles/...`) shows drops and catalog, **but no market/floor prices** — floor is visible only after login.
- **VeVe GraphQL** (`web.api.prod.veve.me/graphql`) is **CSRF/auth-gated**; market queries require an authenticated session.
- **Community trackers** don't fill the gap with a free API:
  - **Veve Alpha** (`vevealpha.com`) tracks both VeVe & StackR floors across ~8,600 items but is a **paid subscription** (free tier = 1 alert, 60-min delay) with **no developer API**.
  - **ecomiwiki.com/veve/market** is a **Cloudflare-protected SPA** (no server-rendered data, no open API).
  - **vevemarket.com** now **301-redirects to VeVe's official site** (defunct as an independent data source).
- **StackR shows a VeVe gem floor, but it too is login-gated (verified 2026-06-26).** StackR (`stackr.world`, a Next.js app) does surface the official VeVe gem-market floor next to its own OMI floor — but **only after VeVe login**. Its API (`stackr.world/api/*`) **redirects to `/connect-veve-auth`**, and its public collectible pages (`stackr.world/collectible/<uuid>`) render the collectible **name only — no floor / gem / OMI values** (the page is a shell full of "Sign In / Connect wallet" prompts). So "just read the VeVe floor off StackR" hits the **same auth wall** as VeVe's own API. Only StackR's **on-chain OMI listings** (via Blockscout, §1) are free of auth.

### Options to obtain a live VeVe floor (owner's choice)

None are free + automated + clearly ToS-clean simultaneously. Ranked by safety:

1. **Manual / imported floors (ToS-clean):** owner enters or pastes VeVe floors (e.g. from the VeVe app or a Veve Alpha export); the app stores them locally (`localStorage`) and uses them. No credentials, no scraping, fully honest. *Recommended default.*
2. **Paid Veve Alpha feed:** if the owner keeps a paid plan, periodically export its floor data into the app's data file. Accurate; depends on a paid third party.
3. **User-supplied VeVe session token (advanced):** the app queries VeVe GraphQL with the owner's own bearer token. Most accurate live data, but **automated access likely violates VeVe's ToS**, tokens expire, and it's fragile — kept **off by default**, behind an explicit warning, if implemented at all.

Until one is chosen, the app shows: **StackR floor** where a listing exists, otherwise the **VeVe drop price** (clearly labelled `~`), and `—` when neither is known. **No estimated VeVe floors are ever shown.**

## See also

- [[architecture]] §6 (floor feed wiring)
- [[Master Collector Points]] · [[Significant Mints]]
- [[collectibles-verified-data]] (provenance / no-invention policy)

platform/market-structure.md:
# Market Structure — VeVe In-App Market vs StackR

The same collectibles trade on **two separate secondary markets**: VeVe's own in-app market, priced in [[Gems]] (1 Gem = US$1), and **StackR** (`stackr.world`), an external marketplace on **Base** that settles in [[OMI Token|OMI]]. They have different currencies, different fee stacks, different depth, and different data visibility — so "the price" of a collectible depends on which venue you are looking at. This page covers how each venue works, what a *floor* means on each, and why a **lowest ask is not a traded price**. For where floor data actually comes from in this project, see [[platform/floor-prices|Floor Prices]]; for real completed sales, see [[platform/record-sales|Record Sales]].

## The two venues side by side

| | **VeVe in-app market** | **StackR** |
|---|---|---|
| Operator | VeVe (in the VeVe app / web app) | StackR — separate marketplace, integrated with VeVe |
| Where it settles | **Collect Chain** — VeVe's purpose-built collectibles chain (full migration completed 2026-04-01) | **Base** (Ethereum L2) |
| Currency | **Gems** (1 Gem = US$1, closed loop) | **OMI** |
| Listing formats | **Fixed price** *and* **24-hour auction** | Fixed **OMI** ask (documented flow) |
| Fixed-price lifetime | Up to **30 days**, auto-removed if unsold | `# TODO` — not published |
| Auctions | 24 h; once a bid lands the auction **cannot be edited or stopped**; highest bid wins, settles automatically | Not documented in StackR's help centre — see callout |
| Who pays fees | **Seller** pays success fees (shown at listing time) | **Seller** pays licensor + marketplace fee; **buyer** pays a fee in OMI |
| Published rates | **VeVe 2.5% + licensor fee when applicable** (VeVe's own example: Marvel 6.0%) | Not published as percentages — shown at listing/purchase |
| Fee destination | VeVe + licensor | Licensors + VeVe; **a percentage of fees is burned** |
| Gas | None (not user-facing) | **None for the user** — StackR sponsors transactions on Base |
| Account requirement | VeVe account | VeVe account **linked** to StackR + a funded OMI wallet |
| Eligible inventory | The whole tradable catalog | **Whitelisted IP only** — availability depends on licensor requirements |
| Price data access | Login-gated (no free public feed) | **Listings are on-chain → publicly indexable** |
| Downtime | Market is taken down around drop time | `# TODO` |

## VeVe in-app market (Gems)

Selling starts from your collection: pick an item and choose **Sell**, then either a fixed price or an auction. On the fixed-price screen VeVe shows **the current floor price for reference, the marketplace success fee, and the exact amount you will receive** once it sells — so net proceeds are disclosed before you commit. Fixed-price listings **stay active for up to 30 days** and are removed automatically if they do not sell. Auctions run a **24-hour** cycle; once a bid is placed the listing cannot be edited or cancelled, and at the end the highest bid wins and settlement is automatic with fees applied.

Fees are **success fees paid by the seller**: a **VeVe fee of 2.5%**, plus a **licensor fee where one applies** — VeVe's own worked example is **Marvel 6.0%**. VeVe's fee schedule states only that secondary-market fees "are displayed to Users at the time that a User lists a Collectible" and "may vary between Collectibles", so treat any single percentage as per-item, not global.

Because Gems are pegged at **1 Gem = US$1**, a Gem ask *is* a USD number with no conversion step. Gems are also, in VeVe's own words, "an in-app licensed product sold by VeVe that is **non-transferable and non-withdrawable**" from **19 November 2025** — see [[Gems]]. That asymmetry matters for anyone thinking of the two venues as arbitrage legs (below).

> [!note] Market downtime around drops
> VeVe has stated it **temporarily takes the marketplace servers down during drop time** so the drop itself runs smoothly. The commonly quoted window of *roughly 30 minutes either side of a drop* is **community documentation ([Vevepedia](https://www.vevepedia.com/terms/marketplace-mp/)), not an official figure** — VeVe publishes no exact duration.

## StackR (OMI on Base)

StackR went live to VeVe's community on **29 April 2025** after about a year in beta, adding an OMI-denominated venue for officially licensed VeVe collectibles. It runs on **Base**, uses **OMI** as its currency, includes a bridge for moving OMI to Base, and **sponsors transactions** so users do not pay gas. You need a VeVe account **linked** to StackR — your collectibles and rankings then show up on StackR — plus OMI in your StackR wallet, which behaves like an ordinary web3 wallet.

The documented listing flow is a **fixed OMI ask**: open your StackR Vault → the collectible's page → **Owned** tab → **Sell for OMI** → enter the OMI amount → **Confirm Listing**, and the listing appears after the on-chain transaction confirms. That **Sell for OMI** pop-up shows the OMI amount corresponding to the **VeVe floor price** as a reference; whether the same comparison appears on StackR's public item pages is `# TODO`.

Fee mechanics are only described qualitatively: transactions carry **licensor and marketplace fees payable by the seller**, plus a **buyer's fee payable in OMI that is permanently removed from circulation**; fees **vary by licensor** (Marvel, Disney, …); and **a percentage of every fee is burned**.

> [!warning] Unverified — StackR's fee rates and who takes them
> The sources do not agree and no percentages are published:
> - VeVe's StackR FAQ says "a small portion goes to licensors and VeVe" and that **StackR does not take a fee**.
> - ECOMI's launch post says transactions include **"licensor and marketplace fees payable by the seller"**.
> - StackR's Terms define a **"Fee" payable to StackR for every Transaction**, disclosed only in the UI at listing/purchase time.
> - A widely repeated third-party figure of "~8.5% on a licensed StackR sale vs ~2.5% with no licensor" comes from a **community blog, not from StackR or VeVe** — do not treat it as a rate card.
> Read the fees on the listing/purchase screen for the specific item. Auction support on StackR is likewise **undocumented** in its help centre; only a fixed-OMI-ask flow is described.

> [!warning] Unverified — custody after the Collect Chain migration
> The 2024 launch material described StackR-traded collectibles as remaining **stored on Immutable X** while accounts updated. VeVe has since migrated to **Collect Chain** (see [[data-landscape-and-apis|Data Landscape & APIs]]), while StackR's listing contracts sit on **Base**. How custody/escrow is arranged post-migration is **not publicly documented**. `# TODO`

## What a "floor" means on each venue

A floor is **the lowest currently active ask** — nothing more. It is venue-specific:

| | VeVe floor | StackR floor |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Lowest live **Gem** ask in the in-app market | Lowest live **OMI** ask on StackR |
| Unit | Gems ≡ USD (1:1, fixed) | OMI, with a USD equivalent **converted at the current OMI rate** |
| Public access | **No free automated source** — login-gated | On-chain listings are public and indexable |
| Stability | Only changes when someone lists/sells/cancels | Also **re-prices in USD terms whenever OMI moves**, with no listing activity at all |

That last row is the structural gotcha: an OMI-denominated ask is *fixed in OMI*, so its dollar-equivalent drifts with the token. Two "floors" quoted in USD are therefore not the same kind of number — the VeVe one is exact by definition, the StackR one is a conversion valid only at its snapshot rate. [[platform/floor-prices|Floor Prices]] documents which of these this project can actually obtain (and the verified fact that VeVe's live in-app floor has no free, ToS-clean automated feed).

## An ask is not a traded price

The single most common error in VeVe valuation is treating a floor as a value.

- **An ask is one person's offer, not a market clearing price.** On an illiquid item a single listing *is* the floor, so one optimistic (or deliberately absurd) ask becomes the quoted "price."
- **Vanity and troll asks are endemic**, especially on desirable mint numbers — which is why this project applies a hard ceiling when it shows "real" prices at all, and why medians are computed on the *lowest* ask per item rather than on all asks.
- **A floor can be unreachable.** If the only supply is in a 24-hour auction, or if the cheapest listing is on the venue you cannot pay on, the floor is not a price you can transact at.
- **Portfolio math built on lowest asks systematically inflates value.** Treat any "collection worth" derived from floors as an upper bound on asks, not an estimate of proceeds — and remember seller fees come off the top.
- **Traded prices exist and should be preferred.** This project's sale history holds **302,286 real completed sales since 2025-07-12** across both venues; [[platform/record-sales|Record Sales]] is built from those, not from asks.

> [!warning] Blind boxes
> Never quote a store/drop/unsold price as the value of a blind box. Only a **real secondary floor** is meaningful; if there is none, quote nothing.

## Liquidity — a measured snapshot

From this project's own listings snapshot, **2026-07-30 09:40 UTC**, **collectibles only** (both venues' harvests exclude comics, so this is not a whole-catalog liquidity figure). StackR asks are quoted natively in OMI; every USD figure below converts at the rate recorded in the same morning's floor snapshot, **OMI/USD = 0.0001528** (2026-07-30 09:04 UTC) — change the rate and every StackR USD number moves with it.

| Metric | VeVe in-app | StackR |
|---|--:|--:|
| Collectibles with ≥1 live ask | 2,301 | 2,260 |
| Live asks, total | 19,199 | 8,524 |
| Mean asks per listed collectible | 8.3 | 3.8 |
| Median *lowest* ask | **$18.90** (Gems) | **100,000 OMI ≈ $15.28** |

Cross-venue, same snapshot:

- **2,511 of ~2,849 catalogued collectibles (≈88%)** carry at least one live ask on at least one venue — so roughly one in eight has **no quote anywhere**, and no floor of any kind.
- **2,050 collectibles are quoted on both venues.** At the rate above, StackR's lowest ask is the cheaper of the two on **1,445 of them (71%)**; the **median StackR ÷ VeVe lowest-ask ratio is 0.83**.
- **Coverage is comparable, depth is not:** StackR quotes almost as many *items* as VeVe but with roughly **half the total asks** and less than half the asks per item — thinner books, so its floor is more easily set by a single listing.
- **No collectible had the same edition number quoted on both venues** (0 of the 2,050). This is consistent with an edition being escrowed to one venue at a time, but that rule is **not published by either operator** — treat it as an observation, not a documented constraint. `# TODO` verify.

> [!note] Snapshot, not a time series
> These are one-moment counts of *active asks*, refreshed by the project's own pipeline. They are not volumes, not trades, and not stable — re-derive before quoting them anywhere, **and re-derive the OMI/USD rate with them**: the StackR-vs-VeVe comparisons are a function of the token price, not of listing behaviour alone.

## Crossing between the venues

VeVe's FAQ is explicit that inventory is fungible across the two markets: collectibles **bought with OMI on StackR can be sold for Gems in VeVe, and vice versa**. The ~17% median ask gap above is therefore *visible* to everyone, which is itself a reason to be suspicious of it as free money. What eats it:

1. **Two different fee stacks**, both seller-side, both licensor-dependent, neither published as a flat rate.
2. **OMI acquisition cost** — spread, slippage and token volatility between buying OMI and settling a trade. A Gem, by contrast, costs exactly $1.
3. **The OMI → Gems path is one-way and lossy**: **$1 of OMI = 1 Gem, minus a 7% OMI burn and a 3% StackR fee** (live since 19 Nov 2025).
4. **Gems do not come back out.** Since 19 Nov 2025 Gems are non-withdrawable, so a gain realised in Gems is **spending power inside VeVe, not cash**.

Point 4 is the one most often skipped: the two venues are not symmetric legs of a trade. OMI → collectible → Gems converts a liquid external asset into closed-loop in-app credit.

> [!warning] Unverified — [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] on StackR
> VeVe's MCP documentation grants a one-off **+15 for a Market purchase**. Whether purchases made on **StackR** earn that (or any) MCP is **not documented**. `# TODO`
