# OMI Economics

**OMI** is the utility token of the ECOMI / **Collect** ecosystem that publishes [[platform/veve|VeVe]]. It is deliberately **not** the app's spending currency — everything inside VeVe is priced in [[Gems]] (1 Gem = US$1) — so OMI's economics are almost entirely about the *outside* of the app: the **StackR** secondary market on Base, the **OMI → Gem** funding path, and the burns attached to both. This page separates what official ECOMI/VeVe/StackR posts actually document from the tokenomics folklore that circulates around it. It contains **no price targets, forecasts, or investment advice**.

## What OMI is — and is not

| | |
|---|---|
| **Ticker / name** | OMI (listed as "ECOMI") |
| **Issuer** | ECOMI, the Singapore-based company behind VeVe ([[platform/ecomi]]). **"ECOMI is rebranding to Collect" is unverified** — no official source found announcing a corporate name change; "Collect" is documented as the chain/platform brand, and the historical rebrand ran the other way (the app "ECOMI Collect" → VeVe) |
| **Token standard** | ERC-20 (Ethereum L1) with deployments on other EVM networks — see below |
| **In-app currency?** | **No.** VeVe Store/Market prices are always in [[Gems]]; Gems are not a cryptoasset and cannot be converted back to OMI |
| **Primary documented utilities** | Buying collectibles on **StackR** (settles in OMI) · **OMI → Gem** conversion · bonus daily [[Master Collector Points\|MCP]] for holding OMI in a linked wallet |
| **Governance token?** | `# TODO` — no official governance mechanism found in VeVe/ECOMI/StackR documentation |

> [!warning] Unverified
> **"OMI is the native/gas token of Collect Chain" is not supported by any official source.** VeVe's own Collect announcement describes a purpose-built collectibles chain with royalties enforced on-chain and mentions OMI only as the thing you *buy Gems with*; it says nothing about gas. The only documented OMI/gas relationship is on **Base**, where StackR operates. Treat the "OMI = gas" claim as community speculation until Collect publishes chain docs.

## Chains and contracts

| Network | Contract | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Ethereum L1 | `0xed35af169af46a02ee13b9d79eb57d6d68c1749e` | Canonical ERC-20; bridge origin |
| Base (L2) | `0x3792DBDD07e87413247DF995e692806aa13D3299` | **StackR settlement + OMI→Gem**; ECOMI-announced (May 2024) |
| Energi | `0x003d765f3793de38ad5ea9d5fd0021cf12c3ba68` | Listed by CoinGecko; **not** documented in the official ECOMI posts reviewed here |

**Lineage:** OMI launched as a **GO-20 token on GoChain**, then swapped **1:1 to ERC-20 on Ethereum** in the migration that began 27 Jan 2022 (announced as the ECOMI × Immutable migration). The 1:1 ratio and the 27 Jan 2022 start are **not stated in ECOMI's own manual-swap guide** (published 12 Jan 2022, procedure only) — both come from exchange migration notices (Gate, AscendEX, BitForex), which agree. Immutable X held the OMI used by VeVe's old in-app "OMI Web Wallet"; per Immutable's own documentation, **Immutable X was merged into Immutable Chain in early 2026**. Movement between Ethereum L1 and Base uses the **StackR bridge** — no cost beyond gas, deposits in roughly 15 block confirmations, and the standard **7-day optimistic-rollup challenge period** on withdrawals back to L1.

> [!warning] Unverified
> The present status of the **IMX-side OMI balance / old in-app OMI wallet** after the Collect migration is unclear. ECOMI's 2025 recap describes rewards for holding OMI in a **StackR self-custody wallet**, while the older MCP pages describe depositing OMI to a **VeVe web wallet on L2**. Which wallet is authoritative in 2026 is `# TODO` — verify in-app before moving tokens.

## Supply

Snapshot from CoinGecko, **2026-07-30** — supply and valuation figures are time-sensitive by nature; this wiki records them dated, not tracked.

| Metric | Value (2026-07-30) |
|---|--:|
| Max supply | 750,000,000,000 OMI |
| Total supply | 310,882,000,000 OMI |
| Circulating supply | 270,952,000,000 OMI |
| Market cap | ~$41.7M |
| Fully diluted valuation | ~$47.8M |

> [!warning] Unverified
> **The "750 billion total supply" figure repeated across exchange explainers conflicts with CoinGecko's reported *total* supply of ~310.9B.** 750B is best read as the **maximum/original** supply. **No official ECOMI page reviewed here reconciles the two numbers**, and no sourced breakdown of the ~439B gap was found — the MEXC tokenomics page cited below carries **no distribution breakdown at all** (no "in-app reserve" or token-sale allocation figures), so the gap is attributed here to nothing. Do not present any derived "total burned to date" figure. That number is `# TODO` until Collect publishes a burn accounting.
>
> Exchange supply figures also disagree with each other: on the same date MEXC showed **305.28B total / 282.56B circulating** against CoinGecko's 310.882B / 270.952B. Treat any single-source supply number as approximate.

## Burn mechanics

### Live and officially documented

| Mechanism | Rate | Venue | Since |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OMI → Gem conversion burn** | **7% of the OMI spent is burned** (plus a **3% operations fee** to StackR); neither changes the number of Gems received | StackR | 19 Nov 2025, 12:00am PST |
| Conversion rate | **$1 USD worth of OMI = 1 Gem**, quoted before purchase; **Gems cannot be converted back to OMI** | StackR → VeVe | 19 Nov 2025 |
| **Marketplace transaction-fee burn** | "A percentage of every transaction fee is burned" — StackR states it takes **no platform fee** itself and that fees partly fund licensor royalties (paid in USD) | StackR | StackR launch, **28 Apr 2025** |

**No official burn datapoint was found.** The exact StackR marketplace fee percentage, and the share of it that is burned, are **not published** — `# TODO`. Cumulative OMI burned is also unpublished — `# TODO`.

> [!warning] Unverified
> The widely quoted first-week figure — **"over 100M OMI converted, more than 7M OMI burned"** — is **not attributable to ECOMI**. It does not appear in the OMI→Gem announcement, in VeVe's own OMI-to-Gems post, or in ECOMI's 2025 recap (all three were checked; the recap quantifies nothing, saying only that conversion "quickly became part of regular marketplace activity"). It circulates only in third-party explainers and AI-generated coin pages, and their dating is self-contradictory — at least one places the "first week" as 30 Oct–5 Nov 2025, *before* the 19 Nov 2025 launch. Do not cite it as an official figure. Note that 7M is exactly 7% of 100M, so the pair may simply be a worked example of the burn rate rather than a measurement.

### Historical / likely superseded

The original **OMI Utility Program (OUP) v0.1** (25 Nov 2021, explicitly labelled a work-in-progress) described a very different model: an NFT purchase moved the purchase value in OMI **from the in-app reserve to an "Out of Circulation" wallet**, tiered holders got reduced **buyer burn fees** (0.5% / 0.25% at the "OMI-llionaire" / "OMI-One Kenobi" tiers), and early withdrawal from the program carried a **10% fee that was burned**.

> [!warning] Unverified
> The widely repeated claim that **"10% of VeVe store revenue is used to buy back and burn OMI"** appears in third-party explainers and community analysis, **not** in any current official ECOMI/VeVe page reviewed here. With Gems now closed-loop and the 7% conversion burn in place, treat the 10%-revenue-buyback mechanic as **historical and unconfirmed**. ECOMI's 2026 roadmap language about "more burn mechanisms" is marketing forward-looking language, not a shipped mechanic.

## How OMI is used

| Use | Mechanics | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Buy/sell collectibles on StackR** | StackR runs on **Base**; OMI is the currency for buying, selling and funding wallets. Items bought with OMI on StackR can be sold for Gems in VeVe and vice versa | High — StackR FAQ |
| **Fund in-app spending** | OMI → Gem at $1 = 1 Gem (7% burn + 3% fee), then spend Gems in VeVe | High — ECOMI + VeVe |
| **Bonus daily [[Master Collector Points\|MCP]]** | Holding OMI in the linked wallet earns bonus daily points **pro-rata to holdings against a fixed reward pool**, capped at **10,000,000 eligible OMI** (a *per-season* cap — stated for Season Zero and Season One, not as a standing rule); accrual starts ~24h after deposit and **stops after 7+ days of inactivity**. Seasons also allocated **Bronze Tickets**, sized by average OMI held across the season. The cited pages require OMI in the **omi.veve.me OMI Web Wallet** and explicitly exclude OMI held on Ethereum L1 | Rules verified for Season Zero / Season One (Jan–Mar 2024); the points curve is **not public** and the current-season wallet is `# TODO` (see callout above) |
| **OMI Leaderboard Rewards** | Announced from **1 Sep 2025**: points earned from **OMI burnt during market activity** on StackR; **10M OMI/week** split among the top 25 and **60M OMI/month** among the top 100 (~100M OMI/month total), automatic entry | Announcement verified; **whether it is still running in mid-2026 is `# TODO`** |
| Pricing inside VeVe | **Never** — in-app prices are Gems only | High |

## Staking — read this before believing an APY

There is **no protocol-level OMI staking** in any official ECOMI/VeVe/StackR documentation reviewed here. The official mechanic is **holding**, not locking: OMI sits in your wallet, stays liquid, and earns **MCP points / tickets** (and, for market activity, leaderboard OMI) — not a yield.

> [!warning] Unverified
> Aggregator and exchange pages advertising "ECOMI staking" at double- or triple-digit APY (one lists 213%) are **third-party products or lead-generation pages**, not Collect/ECOMI programs. Any lock-up, rate, or reward they describe is that platform's, with that platform's counterparty risk. Nothing in this wiki should be read as an endorsement of them.

## Where OMI trades

CoinGecko's top venues by 24h volume, **2026-07-30**:

| Venue | Type | Pair | Share of 24h volume |
|---|---|---|--:|
| Deepcoin | CEX | OMI/USDT | 40.6% |
| BingX | CEX | OMI/USDT | 16.5% |
| MEXC | CEX | OMI/USDT | 8.4% |
| MEXC | CEX | OMI/USDC | 5.8% |
| Gate | CEX | OMI/USDT | 5.6% |
| Uniswap V3 (Base) | DEX | OMI/WETH | 4.6% |

Volume is heavily CEX-concentrated: the top venue alone is ~40% of reported 24h volume, and the leading DEX pool is under 5%.

ECOMI's own 2025 recap additionally reports a **Kraken** listing — described as OMI's first access for US, European and Canadian users through a major global platform — **BingX** deposit/withdrawal support on Base, and availability via the **Binance Web3 Wallet**. Kraken did not appear in the CoinGecko top-volume venues on the snapshot date; listings and volumes change constantly, so verify current venues directly.

## Where OMI meets this wiki's market data

VeVe and StackR are **two markets over one catalog** — VeVe's in-app market in Gems, StackR's secondary market in OMI on Base — and both feed the sale history this wiki analyses: **300k+ completed sales since 2025-07-12**, normalised to USD so the two venues are comparable. See [[platform/record-sales]] for the highest recorded sales and [[platform/floor-prices]] for why a "floor" is an *ask*, not a traded price. The economics of the funding path itself (OMI → Gems → collectible) are summarised in [[platform/economy]], and the token concept page is [[OMI Token]].

## Open questions

- Cumulative OMI burned since 19 Nov 2025 — no official running total. `# TODO`
- The exact StackR marketplace fee, its split, and the burned share. `# TODO`
- Whether OMI has any gas or protocol role on **Collect Chain**. `# TODO`
- Whether the **OMI Reward Tier** seasons and **OMI Leaderboard Rewards** are active as of 2026-07. `# TODO`
- Reconciliation of max (750B) vs total (~310.9B) supply. `# TODO`
- Official status of the **Energi** OMI deployment. `# TODO`
- ~~Collect migration timing~~ — **resolved, not an open question.** The Collect announcement *targeted* Phase 1 for **January 2026**; VeVe's own follow-up post, *VeVe Completes Full Migration on Collect Chain*, announces the full catalog migration as complete on **1 April 2026**, with collectscan.com as the chain's block explorer. April 2026 is therefore the **official** completion date, not a third-party claim. **Phase 2 (optional self-custody) remains unshipped** — `# TODO`.

# Platform

The VeVe app and the company behind it.

## What VeVe Is

[[VeVe]] is a mobile-first app and marketplace for officially licensed **digital collectibles**. Collectors buy, display, and trade premium 3D collectibles, digital comics, and digital art from major entertainment brands. Each collectible is a limited, numbered edition. The app emphasizes a polished collecting experience — augmented-reality viewing, virtual "showrooms," and a social/marketplace layer.

## Who Makes It

VeVe is published by [[ECOMI]]. The ecosystem is associated with the [[OMI Token]] cryptocurrency. _(Corporate structure and current branding — to verify against an official source.)_

## Core Features (high level)

- **Store** — primary sales of new [[drops]].
- **Marketplace** — secondary peer-to-peer buying and selling. See [[marketplace]].
- **Showroom** — arrange and display owned collectibles in a virtual room.
- **AR mode** — view collectibles in augmented reality.
- **Comic reader** — read digital comics owned in-app. See [[collectibles]].
- **Gems** — in-app currency used in the store. See [[Gems]].
- **Social** — follow collectors, view their showrooms _(to verify exact feature set)_.

# Rarity System — Tiers, Editions, Mints and Real Supply

VeVe scarcity is built from four independent things that collectors routinely conflate: the **rarity tier** (a label), the **edition size** (how many were issued), the **mint number** (which copy you hold), and the **circulating supply** (how many still exist and are not held back by VeVe). This page walks the whole chain and separates each from the others. Aggregate figures below are computed from this vault's mirror of VeVe's own store data — **2,714 collectible records, snapshot 2026-07-30** — and every per-item field named here (`totalIssued`, `editionsInCirculation`, `withheldEditions`, `editionsBurnt`, `firstAvailableEdition`) is exposed publicly by the storefront itself.

For the conceptual treatment see [[Rarity and Editions]]; this page is the quantitative reference behind it.

## 1. The five rarity tiers

VeVe's official ladder, most common to least:

| # | Tier | Store value | Daily [[Master Collector Points\|MCP]] (collectibles) | Items in mirror |
|---|------|-------------|---:|---:|
| 1 | Common | `COMMON` | 1.00 | 485 |
| 2 | Uncommon | `UNCOMMON` | 1.00 | 365 |
| 3 | Rare | `RARE` | 1.25 | 513 |
| 4 | Ultra Rare | `ULTRA_RARE` | 1.50 | 577 |
| 5 | Secret Rare | `SECRET_RARE` | 6.00 | 663 |

Not every drop spans all five — many sets ship with only one or two tiers. The MCP column is the `dailyMcpPoints` value the store returns, and it was uniform across every item in each tier that reports it (198 of 2,714 records leave the field null; no contradicting value found), which matches VeVe's published collectible scheme exactly: a base of 1.00 per collectible owned plus tier bonuses of +0.25 Rare / +0.50 Ultra Rare / +5.00 Secret Rare. **These values are for collectibles only** — comics run a different published ladder (0.25 Common / 0.5 Uncommon / 2.0 Rare / 3.0 Ultra Rare / 6.0 Secret Rare). Points, not edition size, are where the tier label has its hardest mechanical effect — see [[Master Collector Points]].

### Artist Proof — the sixth value

A sixth rarity value, `ARTIST_PROOF` (**AP**), appears on **111** records in the mirror. Every one of them has an edition size of exactly **1**. AP is the label VeVe uses for 1-of-1 artwork pieces from the VeVe Artworks / artist program, typically sold by silent auction rather than at a fixed store price. AP sits outside the Common→Secret Rare ladder rather than above it, and pays the base 1.00 MCP/day.

## 2. Typical edition sizes per tier

Edition size is set per item at drop time and never changes upward — once all editions are issued, no more are minted. Across the mirror:

| Tier | Items | Median issued | Mean | 10th pct | 90th pct | Min | Max |
|------|------:|--------------:|-----:|---------:|---------:|----:|----:|
| Common | 485 | 2,018 | 5,383 | 77 | 13,928 | 1 | 92,072 |
| Uncommon | 365 | 2,025 | 3,781 | 955 | 9,000 | 59 | 25,090 |
| Rare | 513 | 1,888 | 2,583 | 675 | 6,000 | 44 | 25,000 |
| Ultra Rare | 577 | 964 | 1,487 | 400 | 3,400 | 29 | 12,500 |
| Secret Rare | 663 | 355 | 797 | 66 | 1,955 | 1 | 10,000 |
| Artist Proof | 111 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

Three things worth reading off that table:

- **Common and Uncommon are statistically indistinguishable by edition size** (medians 2,018 vs 2,025). The real separation only begins at Ultra Rare, and only becomes dramatic at Secret Rare.
- **The ranges overlap enormously.** The largest Secret Rare in the mirror is 10,000 editions; the smallest Common is 1. A 10,000-edition Secret Rare is more numerous than 90% of Ultra Rares.
- **Means run far above medians** in every tier — a handful of mass-market items (a 92,072-edition Common, a 70,000-edition tiered giveaway) drag the average. Use the median.

## 3. Rarity is relative *within a set*, not an absolute

This is the single most misread part of the system. A tier label tells you where an item sits in **its own drop**, not how it compares to anything else in the catalog. Vevepedia states plainly that "rarities do not necessarily correspond to edition size." Note the attribution: VeVe's own marketplace explainer names the five tiers but makes no statement either way, so this is a well-evidenced community reading rather than a published VeVe rule — the evidence for it is the data below.

Testing that against the data: of the **459** multi-tier sets in the mirror, **413 (90.0%)** have median edition size that never rises as rarity rises — the expected shape. **46 sets (10.0%) violate it outright.**

| Set | Common | Uncommon | Rare | Ultra Rare | Secret Rare |
|-----|-------:|---------:|-----:|-----------:|------------:|
| DEADBEATS – Series One | 7,777 | 6,777 | 4,777 | **1,777** | **5,000** |
| Rogue | 2,500 | **3,000** | 1,900 | 800 | 300 |
| RUNNING MON Series 2 | 790 | **990** | 690 | 390 | 190 |
| CIARA Series 1 | 800 | **999** | 699 | — | 199 |

The DEADBEATS row is the instructive one. Its Secret Rare (**Melvin**, 5,000 editions) is nearly three times more numerous than the set's Ultra Rare (Andy, 1,777) — and Melvin is nonetheless the **highest recorded sale in the entire vault sale window at $44,999** ([[platform/record-sales|record sales]]). Tier label, edition size, and market value are three separate axes.

## 4. Mint numbers

Every copy carries a unique **mint number** within its edition — "#41 of 1,200". Mint number is a property of your specific copy, not of the collectible, and it is the axis where collectors pay the steepest premiums: low mints, #1s, ceiling mints, palindromes, meme numbers, and character-meaningful years. That whole taxonomy lives in [[Significant Mints]]; community-observed premium multiples over floor are catalogued in [[Rarity and Editions]].

## 5. Reserved low mints (withheld editions)

VeVe holds a block of editions back from public sale for licensors, promotional and team distribution, and giveaways. The consequence: **the lowest mint you can actually buy is usually not #1.**

`firstAvailableEdition` — the lowest publicly minted edition — across the 2,446 records that report it:

| First public mint | Items | Share | Implied reserve below it |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **#41** | 1,332 | 54.5% | 40 |
| **#21** | 547 | 22.4% | 20 |
| **#1** | 147 | 6.0% | 0 (no reserve) |
| #6 | 131 | 5.4% | 5 |
| #11 | 87 | 3.6% | 10 |
| #42 | 42 | 1.7% | 41 |
| #31 | 33 | 1.3% | 30 |
| #16 | 29 | 1.2% | 15 |
| other (26 more values) | 98 | 4.0% | up to 192 |

So **#41 is the modal answer and the median reserve is exactly 40** — but it is only true just over half the time, 34 distinct values occur, and roughly one item in sixteen has no reserve at all. **Never assume #41 for a specific item; read its `firstAvailableEdition`.**

> [!note] Withheld total ≠ reserve depth
> Announced withheld counts are **per rarity pool, not per item**, so they cannot be read off any single item's first public mint. In the Lamborghini 350 GT drop VeVe states: "A total of 90 editions from the Rare and Ultra Rare collectibles will be withheld by VeVe for licensor, promotional, team and comp distribution" — 90 across *three* items (Rosso, Rare, 1,200; Azzurro and Blu Scuro, Ultra Rare, 964 each) — plus a separate **40** from the Secret Rare pool (Verde Scuro, 120). All four report a first public edition of **#41**.
> That cuts against the intuitive reading: 90 withheld is *fewer* than the 120 editions sitting below #41 across those three items. The two are simply different quantities and neither bounds the other. Separately, the mirror reports `withheldEditions: 0` for all four of these items today — the field is a **live residual**, not the drop-time reserve, which is why the §7 withheld bucket is so small.

> [!warning] Unverified
> Whether VeVe also withholds scattered mints from *above* the first public edition for marketing is **# TODO** — no source consulted states this.

## 6. Burnt editions

Unsold store inventory can be **burned** — permanently destroyed, reducing supply forever. VeVe has run this both as one-off announced burn events (e.g. the Marvel collectibles and comics burn of 31 Oct 2024) and as standing policy: since **1 March 2025**, Marvel / Disney / Star Wars backlist digital comics sell for a **30-day window** only, after which the remainder is burned, so the final edition count reflects actual demand rather than the printed ceiling.

Burning is not marginal. In the mirror, **629 of 2,714 items (23%) have a non-zero burn count**, and **703,270 editions — 10.5% of all issued supply — have been destroyed.** (The ledger in §7 shows a slightly smaller 699,922 because it excludes the records described in the caveats.)

| Tier | Items with burns | Editions burnt | % of tier's issued supply |
|------|---:|---:|---:|
| Common | 139 / 485 | 214,203 | 8.2% |
| Uncommon | 118 / 365 | 138,900 | 10.1% |
| Rare | 125 / 513 | 125,776 | 9.5% |
| Ultra Rare | 122 / 577 | 69,957 | 8.1% |
| Secret Rare | 125 / 663 | 154,434 | **29.2%** |
| Artist Proof | 0 / 111 | 0 | 0.0% |

The Secret Rare figure is not evidence that SRs burn more readily — it is concentration. A handful of 10,000-edition SR items sold through only a sliver of their run and had the rest destroyed, which dominates a tier whose median edition is 355.

The extremes reshape an item completely:

| Collectible | Tier | Issued | Burnt | Actually circulating |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| AMC Tyrannosaurus rex | Common | 35,090 | 30,285 (86.3%) | **4,805** |
| JENNIE – Cool Command | Common | 14,000 | 13,849 (98.9%) | **101** |
| The Tiniest Bit of Greed | Secret Rare | 10,000 | 9,894 (98.9%) | **106** |
| UCI Germany Tyrannosaurus rex | Common | 10,090 | 10,000 (99.1%) | **90** |

A "Common with 14,000 editions" of which 101 survive is, in every way that matters to scarcity, a triple-digit item.

## 7. Issued vs circulating vs held — the supply ledger

VeVe's store data separates the ceiling from reality, and the identity closes exactly. Over the **2,496** records reporting positive circulation:

| Bucket | Editions | Share of issued |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Total issued** (the printed ceiling) | 6,217,260 | 100.0% |
| — in circulation | 5,490,465 | 88.3% |
| — withheld by VeVe | 26,873 | 0.4% |
| — burnt | 699,922 | 11.3% |

`totalIssued = editionsInCirculation + withheldEditions + editionsBurnt` held with **zero residual** across all 2,496 items, so these three buckets are exhaustive.

One further subtlety: **"in circulation" is not the same as "in collectors' hands."** Of those 5,490,465 circulating editions, **691,031 (12.6%)** are still unsold stock sitting in the VeVe store across 809 items. Circulation counts everything that exists and is neither reserved nor destroyed — including inventory nobody has bought yet.

The practical hierarchy, tightest to loosest:

```
edition size printed on the item   (totalIssued)
  ├─ minus burnt                   → supply that will ever exist
  ├─ minus withheld                → supply the public could ever own
  └─ minus unsold store stock      → supply actually held by collectors
```

Any scarcity claim, floor comparison, or portfolio valuation should say which of those four numbers it is using. [[platform/floor-prices|Floor prices]] in particular are lowest-*ask* listings, not traded values, and get noisy on items whose real circulating count is small.

## 8. Why it matters

- **Value.** Scarcity is priced across all four axes at once. Tier, surviving edition count, and mint number each carry independent premiums, which is why a Common can out-sell a Secret Rare — see [[platform/record-sales]] for real examples of exactly that.
- **Points.** Tier drives daily [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] directly (Secret Rare at 6.00/day is 6× a Common), with a bonus for the lowest 5% of mints. Duplicates diminish in **both** categories: collectible duplicates of the same item pay 0.75 / 0.35 / 0.10 points for the 2nd / 3rd / 4th-and-later copy, and comic duplicates of the same issue pay 50% / 25% / 10% of daily points — with Common and Uncommon comics exempt from diminishing entirely.
- **Chase mechanics.** [[Blind Box|Blind boxes]] exist to make the top tier a lottery; the [[Secret Rare]] is the pull that drives the format. See [[platform/drops]] for how tiers are allocated at drop time.
- **Two markets.** The same edition trades in VeVe's in-app market in [[Gems]] (1 Gem = 1 USD) and on StackR, the secondary market on Base settling in [[OMI Token|OMI]]. Scarcity is one asset; the price discovery happens in two places.

> [!warning] Data caveats
> - Figures are a **2026-07-30 snapshot** of VeVe's store data as mirrored in this vault (2,714 collectible records). The live catalog is larger — roughly 2,850 collectibles plus ~3,856 comic issues — and comics are not included in the tables above. Numbers move with every drop and every burn.
> - **218 records were excluded from the supply ledger**: 216 report zero circulation (unreleased items, poster/reward records, and fully-withheld tiered giveaways), and **2 report a negative circulation value** ("Larry the Lobster" and its box, at −1,625 and −1,723) — an upstream data artifact, not a real quantity. One further item reports unsold stock exceeding its own circulation.
> - `firstAvailableEdition` is absent on 268 records; the reserve table covers only the 2,446 that report it. The #1–40 reserve is **practice, not published rule**: the only source found is Vevepedia — an unofficial fan site, "in no way officially affiliated with VeVe or ECOMI" — which says "VeVe holds back a small number of collectibles for the licensors and for marketing purposes, the lowest mint numbers for most collectibles in 41", and that "earlier collectibles in the app can have lower mint numbers due to VeVe holding back fewer collectibles at the time." **No statement by VeVe** on the reserve's size, its history, or whether it may change was found.
> - Edition-size and burn aggregates are descriptive of this snapshot only. They are **not** a rule about what a future drop will do.

platform/seasons.md:
# Seasons

VeVe groups its collectible releases into numbered **Seasons**, running from Season 1 (opened October 2020 with Batman Black & White #100) through **Season 12**, live as of mid-2026. A Season is attached to a **collectible series**, not to an individual item and not to a calendar quarter — which is why seasons overlap in wall-clock time and why a handful of items carry a season number far older than their drop date. Comics are outside the system entirely: they carry no season at all.

## What a Season is

VeVe's own framing is about collector identity rather than mechanics. The platform describes grouping collectible releases into seasons as "set to become an essential part of a VeVe collector's identity," and points at your first collectible as the thing that "pinpoints that special moment in time when you started your digital collection." Season 1 was explicitly the proving ground — VeVe says it "trialed and tested a number of releases, edition numbers, and other mechanisms."

What a Season is **not**:

- **Not a rewards period.** It does not gate points, tickets or airdrops — see [[#Not to be confused with — OMI Rewards Seasons]].
- **Not a rarity or edition attribute.** Season is orthogonal to [[Rarity and Editions|rarity and edition size]].
- **Not a set.** A [[platform/drops|drop]]/set is one release event; a Season is the release *window* that contains many of them.
- **Not a strict date bucket.** See [[#Seasons are not date buckets]].

## Where Season appears

Season is surfaced publicly and mirrored into this wiki:

| Surface | How it appears |
|---|---|
| VeVe series page (`veve.me/collectibles/en/series/…`) | `Season` row in the **Details** block, alongside Drop Date, Market Fee, License, Brand |
| VeVe collectible page (`…/collectibles/…`) | Same `Season` row, plus List Price, Daily MCP Points, Drop Type |
| VeVe comic page (`…/comics/…`) | **Absent** — no Season field |
| This wiki | `season:` frontmatter key on `wiki/collectibles/` and `wiki/collections/` pages |

In the wiki the value is joined `collect_id → series → series_season` by `tools/backfill_season.py`, so a collectible's season is always inherited from its series rather than guessed from its drop date.

> [!note] Season is a property of the series
> Across the 851 collectible series in the catalogue export, **zero** series carried more than one season value. Every item in a series shares the series' season, however long that series takes to finish dropping.

## Season timeline

Derived from the taxonomy export (snapshot 2026-06-26; 2,492 collectibles across 851 series, covering drops 2020-10-14 → 2026-04-19). Every row in that export carried a numeric season, spanning Seasons 1–11.

"First tagged drop" is the earliest drop date of any item bearing that season — a **lower bound** on the season's true opening, not a VeVe-published boundary. "Bulk through" is roughly the 95th percentile of drop dates, which is a better guide to when the season stopped being the live one.

| Season | First tagged drop | Bulk through (~95th pct) | Last tagged drop | Series | Items |
|--:|---|---|---|--:|--:|
| **1** | 2020-10-14 | 2021-05-13 | 2024-10-31 | 21 | 93 |
| **2** | 2021-05-20 | 2021-10-09 | 2021-12-18 | 31 | 102 |
| **3** | 2021-10-16 | 2022-04-17 | 2022-05-07 | 82 | 252 |
| **4** | 2022-05-15 | 2022-10-09 | 2022-10-15 | 72 | 195 |
| **5** | 2022-10-16 | 2023-05-01 | 2023-05-15 | 116 | 268 |
| **6** | 2023-05-19 | 2023-10-17 | 2023-11-26 | 85 | 215 |
| **7** | 2023-10-27 | 2024-04-28 | 2024-05-13 | 81 | 220 |
| **8** | 2024-05-16 | 2024-10-18 | 2025-12-05 | 94 | 227 |
| **9** | 2024-10-26 | 2025-05-16 | 2025-07-20 | 109 | 368 |
| **10** | 2025-05-17 | 2025-10-11 | 2026-01-31 | 71 | 228 |
| **11** | 2025-10-25 | 2026-04-06 | 2026-04-19 | 89 | 324 |
| **12** | 2026-05-16 *(earliest verified)* | — | — | `# TODO` | `# TODO` |

Season 12 is confirmed live on the public storefront but sits **after** the export snapshot, so its counts are unknown here. The Season 12 items verified directly are *Imperial Royal Guard* (Star Wars / Dark Side Collection, drop 16 May 26), *Turtle Cycle* (TMNT, drop 17 Jun 26) and *Team Avatar: SDCC 2026* (drop 23 Jul 26, still Season 12).

> [!warning] Unverified — exact season boundaries
> VeVe has published a boundary date for exactly one season: Season 1 ran from the 15 October 2020 Batman Black & White #100 release to a final drop on **13 May 2021** (the tokidoki Dragon Girl release). Every other opening date in the table above is *inferred* from the earliest drop carrying that season number, and the true switchover could fall days earlier. No VeVe post found states a full Season 1–12 boundary table, or a policy for how long a season runs. Treat the first/last columns as observed extremes, not official dates.
>
> The Season 1 opening also differs by a day between sources — VeVe says 15 October 2020, the export records `2020-10-14 15:00 UTC`. These are the same moment read in different timezones (15:00 UTC on the 14th is early on the 15th in New Zealand, where VeVe is based), but the wiki records the export value on collectible pages.

## The observed six-month cadence

Season openings are strikingly regular: **two per year, one in mid-May and one in mid-to-late October**, holding without a break across all twelve seasons.

| Year | ~May opening | ~October opening |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | — | S1 (14 Oct) |
| 2021 | S2 (20 May) | S3 (16 Oct) |
| 2022 | S4 (15 May) | S5 (16 Oct) |
| 2023 | S6 (19 May) | S7 (27 Oct) |
| 2024 | S8 (16 May) | S9 (26 Oct) |
| 2025 | S10 (17 May) | S11 (25 Oct) |
| 2026 | S12 (16 May) | `# TODO` |

> [!warning] Unverified — the cadence is an observation, not a policy
> This pattern is read off the data; **no VeVe source found states that seasons are six months long or that they open in May and October.** It has held for twelve consecutive seasons, which makes an October 2026 Season 13 a reasonable expectation — but this wiki does not assert it, and the cadence could change at any time.

## Why seasons overlap in wall-clock time

Because the season is fixed on the *series*, a multi-item series that keeps dropping items for months carries its original season number the whole way. The result is that every season has a **long thin tail** of items dropping after the next season has already opened:

- Season 2's last tagged item dropped 2021-12-18 — two months after Season 3 had opened.
- Season 8 opened 2024-05-16 but has an item dated 2025-12-05, roughly 19 months later.
- Every season has items after its ~95th-percentile date, typically 4–16 of them.

Practical consequence: **you cannot infer a season from a drop date, or a drop date from a season.** For per-item dates the wiki uses the `nft_drop_date` field, which is independent of `season` (and independent again of `comic_debut` — see the field definitions in `CLAUDE.md`).

## Seasons are not date buckets

The clearest counterexample is verifiable on VeVe's own storefront. The **Cryptkins - Midnight Chupacabra Series** shows a drop date of `31 Oct 24` and `Season: 1` — a 2024 drop labelled Season 1, three and a half years after Season 1's other items. The export agrees with the public page, so this is genuine platform metadata, not a mirror artefact.

`# TODO` — why this series retains Season 1 is not documented. A legacy/re-issue series inheriting its original season number is the obvious guess, but no source confirms it, so the wiki records the fact and not the explanation.

A second wrinkle: the Season field is not rendered on every series page. A sampled auction-style art series (*Skottie Young - X-Men '92 #1*) displayed only Auction Closes / Artist / Brand / Series, with no Season row, even though the export assigns it Season 7. Whether that is specific to auction or art formats is `# TODO` — two sampled pages is not enough to generalise.

## Why comics carry no season

Comics sit outside the season system on both the data side and the UI side:

- **Schema.** The comics taxonomy export has 84 columns and **not one contains "season"** — the field simply does not exist for comics, whereas the collectibles export has `series_season` populated on every row.
- **Public UI.** A sampled comic page (*The Avengers #43*, drop 29 Apr 25) shows Writers, Artists, Cover Artists, Characters, Publisher, Series, Issue, Start Year, Pages, List Price, Market Fee, Drop Type, Available — **no Season**.

Comics are organised by *publication* identity instead: publisher → comic series → issue number → start year, plus the original print publication date. That is a real-world bibliographic axis, and it does not need VeVe's release-window axis to sit on top of it. So the wiki's `season` key appears only on collectible and collectible-collection pages; comic pages leave it off entirely rather than filling it with a guess.

`# TODO` — no VeVe statement was found explaining the omission; the two facts above are the evidence, the reasoning is inference.

## Not to be confused with — OMI Rewards Seasons

The [[Master Collector Points|Master Collector Program]] runs its own, separately numbered **OMI Rewards Seasons**, and they are a completely different clock. OMI Rewards Season Two ran **1 April 2024 → 30 June 2024** — a three-month quarter — while collectible Season 8 opened 16 May 2024 in the middle of it. The two numberings are independent and should never be cross-referenced.

| | Collectible Season | OMI Rewards Season |
|---|---|---|
| Attached to | a collectible series | a user's OMI holdings period |
| Length | ~6 months (observed) | ~3 months (quarterly) |
| Numbering at mid-2026 | 12 | `# TODO` |
| Governs | catalogue organisation, collector identity | bonus MCP points, Bronze Tickets, airdrops |
| Applies to comics | no | yes (comics earn MCP) |

> [!warning] Unverified — the current OMI Rewards season number
> VeVe's published OMI Rewards posts stop at **Season Two** (1 April → 30 June 2024), which names **Season Three** as opening 1 July 2024 but gives it no end date. No post announcing Season Four or later was found, and no announcement that the program ended was found either. So the OMI Rewards season number as of mid-2026 is unknown: if the quarterly cadence simply continued it would be around Season Eleven, which is *close to* the collectible Season number by coincidence. Do not read the two numberings as related, and do not assume OMI Rewards is still running in seasons.

## Open questions

- `# TODO` Official boundary dates for Seasons 2–12.
- `# TODO` Whether VeVe has ever stated an intended season length.
- `# TODO` Why some series retain an out-of-era season number (Cryptkins Season 1).
- `# TODO` Which formats suppress the Season row in the storefront Details block.
- `# TODO` Season 12 series/item counts, once the taxonomy export is refreshed past 2026-04-19.
- `# TODO` Whether Season correlates with anything economically interesting (floor behaviour, [[platform/record-sales|record sales]] concentration) — an analysis, not a fact, and not yet run.

## Sources

- https://medium.com/veve-collectibles/the-seasons-they-are-a-changin-6d74e4379785 — VeVe's own Season 1 retrospective: Batman Black & White #100 on 15 October 2020 as the first collectible, 13 May 2021 final Season 1 drop, seasons as collector identity
- https://www.veve.me/collectibles/en/series/a8443de7-4a0e-4110-aee8-8387b672bccf — *VeVe Early Days* series page: `Season: 11`, drop 15 Nov 25
- https://www.veve.me/collectibles/en/series/9c52ab4f-172b-4395-8ca9-2bc0637351a3 — *Cryptkins - Midnight Chupacabra Series*: `Season: 1`, drop 31 Oct 24 (the out-of-era case)
- https://www.veve.me/collectibles/en/series/5880f307-d899-400c-bf02-ba85b3b87bf7 — *Imperial Royal Guard* (Star Wars): `Season: 12`, drop 16 May 26
- https://www.veve.me/collectibles/en/collectibles/f5a9fdc5-7bbb-4ac0-85da-8e85028f6840 — *Turtle Cycle* (TMNT): `Season: 12`, drop 17 Jun 26, full Details block
- https://www.veve.me/collectibles/en/collectibles/39e873a8-37f3-4ef8-9247-b2b257f7dcbf — *Team Avatar: SDCC 2026*: `Season: 12`, drop 23 Jul 26 — confirms Season 12 was still the live season in late July 2026
- https://www.veve.me/collectibles/en/series/9ecfa9fa-1f01-440a-aba3-d308126c97a0 — *Skottie Young - X-Men '92 #1*: Details block with no Season row
- https://www.veve.me/collectibles/en/comics/7bff0176-7ccf-491d-b6ed-ec90174b5c37 — *The Avengers #43* comic page: Details block confirming comics show no Season
- https://www.veve.me/blog/veve/mcp/veve-master-collector-program-omi-rewards-season-two/ — OMI Rewards Season Two, 1 April 2024 → 30 June 2024 (the separate quarterly cycle); also states Season Three opens 1 July 2024. The old `blog.veve.me/post/…` form of this URL now redirects to a 404

platform/veve.md:
# VeVe

**VeVe** is the digital-collectibles app at the centre of this wiki — a mobile-first marketplace for officially licensed **collectibles** (3D Premium Collectibles, comics, and digital art) from 50+ licensors (Marvel, DC, Star Wars, Disney, and more). See the [[platform/platform|Platform]] overview for features.

## Key facts
- **Maker:** [[ecomi|ECOMI]], now rebranding to **Collect**. *(high)*
- **Launched:** 2018 (as the ECOMI app); first Marvel Spider-Man NFT Aug 2021. *(high)*
- **Chain:** GoChain → Immutable X (2021) → **Collect Chain** (full migration ~early 2026). On-chain data via [[data-landscape-and-apis|collectscan]]. *(high)*
- **Currency:** [[Gems]] (1 Gem = US$1, closed-loop); ecosystem token [[OMI Token|OMI]] (converts to Gems on StackR — a *separate* Base marketplace). *(high)*
- **Mechanics:** timed [[platform/drops|drops]] (incl. [[Blind Box|blind boxes]]), a secondary [[platform/marketplace|marketplace]], [[Rarity and Editions|rarity tiers & mint numbers]], and the [[Master Collector Points|Master Collector Program]].

## Connections
- Company → [[ecomi|ECOMI / Collect]]
- How it works → [[platform/platform|Platform]] · [[platform/drops|Drops]] · [[platform/marketplace|Marketplace]] · [[economy]]
- Catalog → [[collectibles/_index|Collectibles]]

## Sources
- [[data-landscape-and-apis]], [[catalog-rarity-drops]]

platform/veve-history.md:
# VeVe History — Timeline

A dated timeline of [[veve|VeVe]] and its parent [[ecomi|ECOMI / Collect]]: the token that came before the app, the October 2020 first drop, the 2021 licensing boom (Marvel, DC, Disney, Star Wars), [[platform/collectibles|VeVe Comics]], and the two blockchain migrations — GoChain → Immutable X → **Collect Chain**. Every entry below is anchored to a month or day taken from an official announcement, contemporaneous press, or this wiki's own catalog data; anything that could not be pinned down is marked `# TODO` or flagged in a callout.

## At a glance

| Era | Period | Defining event |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-app | 2017–2019 | ECOMI founded; ECOMI Secure Wallet; OMI token IEO |
| Launch | Oct 2020 – Apr 2021 | First collectibles drop (Batman Black & White Series 1); [[Rarity and Editions\|Season 1]] |
| The boom | May 2021 – Dec 2021 | Marvel, Disney, Star Wars, USPS; 1M+ monthly users; move to Immutable X |
| Build-out | 2022–2023 | Showrooms, [[platform/drops\|drop]] formats, catalog expansion |
| Comics | Mar 2024 | VeVe Comics launches with Marvel |
| Ecosystem | Feb 2025 – Nov 2025 | VeVeVerse; StackR secondary market; Collect Chain announced |
| Collect Chain | Jan 2026 – Apr 2026 | Migration completes; collectscan.com explorer |

## 2017–2019 — before the app

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Apr 2017 | **ECOMI founded** — **co-founded by David Yu and Dan Crothers**; VeVe's own April 2026 release styles Yu "Co-Founder and CEO". Headquartered in Singapore. The operating entity is ORBIS Blockchain Technologies Ltd, registered in New Zealand (NZ company no. 6545833) with offices in Auckland. |
| 2019 | **ECOMI Secure Wallet** — a credit-card-sized cold-storage hardware wallet — is ECOMI's first shipped product, predating VeVe. |
| 12–13 May 2019 | **OMI token IEO on BitForex.** OMI launched as a **GO20 token on GoChain**; the subscription opened 12 May 2019 (21:00 GMT+8) and sold out at 08:52 GMT+8 on 13 May 2019, with OMI/BTC trading from 15 May. Total supply 750 billion. The BitForex subscription offered **10 billion OMI against a 100 BTC hard cap**; the **150 billion (20% of supply)** figure is the *circulating supply at launch*, not the amount sold in the IEO. |

> [!warning] Unverified
> **Founding date and HQ.** Vevepedia and Gate's research page both state **April 2017, Singapore**, and Vevepedia credits **David Yu alone** as "founder & CEO". Other secondary write-ups (Coin Bureau, Coinspeaker) say ECOMI was "founded in 2018"; **Wikipedia says VeVe was founded in 2018 by Dan Crothers and David Yu, Auckland**; and this wiki's own [[ecomi|ECOMI]] page currently says *2018, Auckland*. The **co-founder** reading is the better-sourced one — VeVe's April 2026 migration release calls Yu "Co-Founder and CEO", and NZ court records name both Yu and Daniel Crothers alongside ORBIS. The **year** remains unsettled: no incorporation date was verified, so 2017 is recorded here as the best-sourced figure rather than a settled one.
>
> **OMI's origin date.** Coinspeaker states the token "came into existence in June 2018 following an IEO on BitForex"; GoChain's own partner announcement and ICO Drops both place the BitForex IEO in **May 2019**. ICOholder additionally cites a token-generation event concluding 15 Dec 2019. These cannot all be true; the May 2019 IEO is the version with a first-party source (GoChain).

## 2020 — VeVe launches

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **14 Oct 2020** | **First collectibles on VeVe: *Batman Black & White* Series 1** (DC). The set comprised four statues, **each a different rarity and edition size**: *#01 Eduardo Risso* (Ultra Rare, 1,750 @ 69.99 Gems), *#86 Becky Cloonan* (Rare, 3,250 @ 49.99), *#97 Joe Madureira* (Uncommon, 5,500 @ 44.99) and *#100 Todd McFarlane* (Common, 7,500 @ 79.99). VeVe's own five-year retrospective names *Batman Black & White* Series 1 as the app's opening drop but dates it only to **October 2020**; the day-level 14 Oct date comes from this wiki's catalog, which holds no earlier drop. |
| Late 2020 | The in-app **[[platform/marketplace\|Market]]** opens shortly after launch, enabling peer-to-peer resale. VeVe's retrospective says only "soon after"; no dated announcement was located. |

> [!warning] Unverified
> Several secondary sources (Coin Bureau, Gate, NFT Evening) say the VeVe **app** "went live in December 2020"; Wikipedia instead puts VeVe's founding and launch in **2018**. VeVe's own retrospective dates the **first collectible drop** to October 2020 and this wiki's catalog to 14 Oct 2020. These claims may describe different events (founding vs. limited release vs. general availability); the exact public-launch date of the app itself is `# TODO`.
>
> Bleeding Cool dates a DC *Batman Black & White* VeVe launch to **11 March 2021**. Every Series 1 item in this wiki's catalog carries `nft_drop_date: 2020-10-14`, so the March 2021 article most likely covers a later Batman series rather than Series 1.
>
> **Batman Series 1 drop prices look internally inconsistent.** The catalog prices the *Common* (7,500 editions) highest at 79.99 Gems and the *Ultra Rare* (1,750) lower at 69.99 — inverted from VeVe's normal rarity/price relationship. Edition sizes and rarities are as recorded above; the **Gem prices are `# TODO`** pending a check against the original drop announcement.

## 2021 — the boom

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **28 Jan 2021** | First **Ghostbusters** collectibles — *Mooglie (Ghostbusters Logo)*, the *Ghostbusters I Logo* and the *Stay Puft Marshmallow Man*. *Mooglie Platinum* (200 editions, 89 Gems) and *Ghostbusters I Logo – Platinum* (200 editions) are the **earliest [[Secret Rare]]s in this wiki's catalog**, tied on the same day. |
| **13 May 2021** | **Season 1 ends** — its final drop is tokidoki artist Simone Legno's *Dragon Girl*. VeVe publishes *"The Seasons, They Are a-Changin'"* (15 May 2021), framing Season 1 as the platform's trial/beta era and its items as "OG" collectibles. Season 2 drops begin the following week (earliest Season 2 item in this wiki's catalog: 20 May 2021). |
| **29 May 2021** | **ECOMI announces the move to Ethereum via Immutable X**, leaving GoChain for a gas-free Ethereum L2. |
| **5 Aug 2021** | Marvel Entertainment and Orbis Blockchain Technologies announce **Marvel's first official NFTs**, on Spider-Man. |
| **7 Aug 2021** | ***Modern Marvel Series 1 — Spider-Man*** drops. Five statues, matching this wiki's catalog exactly: *The Amazing Spider-Man* (Common, 32,000 @ 40 Gems), *Hangin' Out* (Uncommon, 16,000 @ 50), *Jump Into Action* (Rare, 9,000 @ 100), *Animated* (Ultra Rare, 2,500 @ 250), *Ultimate Animated* (Secret Rare, 1,000 @ 400). |
| Aug 2021 | **First licensed classic comics.** *Marvel Comics #1* makes its digital debut on VeVe, with the inaugural classic-comics series beginning 19 Aug 2021. |
| 28 Sep 2021 | **Immutable X rollout plan published.** Phase 1 (wallet registration) and Phase 2 (NFT re-minting) are marked complete; Phase 3 (swapping GoChain OMI / wOMI to L1 or L2 ERC-20 OMI) is "intended" for October 2021. |
| 28 Oct 2021 | **Disney and VeVe announce their collaboration**, timed to Disney+ Day on 12 November. |
| 2 Nov 2021 | **First USPS digital stamp art** — a Día de los Muertos series. |
| **7–12 Nov 2021** | ***Disney Golden Moments*** rolls out one drop per day, mostly at 60 Gems: **Homer & Bart and the Skateboard — VeVe's first Simpsons collectibles (7 Nov)**, Mickey's Sorcerer's Hat and Elsa (8 Nov), WALL·E and Pizza Planet Truck (9 Nov), Iron Man and the Avengers Logo (10 Nov), **C-3PO and R2-D2 — VeVe's first Star Wars collectibles** (11 Nov), and *The Partners Statue* (Ultra Rare, 4,333 editions @ 333 Gems) on Disney+ Day, 12 Nov. ECOMI's November 2021 update confirms the collection carried the first-ever digital collectibles from **The Simpsons, Pixar, Star Wars and Disney**. |
| Nov 2021 | **DesignerCon Anaheim** — VeVe's first in-person event, a 3-day weekend with 15 exclusive drops. |
| Nov 2021 | **Scale milestone:** VeVe passes **1 million active monthly users** with **2.6M+ NFTs sold** cumulatively, including **660,000+ in November alone**. |
| **14–15 Dec 2021** | **NFT re-minting on Immutable X completes.** VeVe's own channels announce "Re-minting 100%" with market and transfers restored; contemporaneous coverage (15 Dec 2021) reports **2.6M+ premium NFTs** moved to Ethereum L2, carbon-neutral and gas-free via Immutable X + StarkWare. The same announcement notes the **OMI token swap would not happen until after the new year** — so the NFT migration and the token migration completed at different times. |

> [!warning] Unverified
> **OMI's 2021 all-time high is disputed.** Price trackers variously report ~$0.0084 (10 Oct 2021), ~$0.0136 (19 Mar 2021) and ~$0.01344. Because these figures come from aggregators that disagree with one another and depend on which exchange feed is used, no ATH is asserted here.
>
> **Phase 3 (the OMI token swap) slipped.** The 28 Sep 2021 rollout plan stated an *intention* to finish Phase 3 in October 2021. It did not: VeVe's own December 2021 re-minting announcement says the token swap "will not happen until after the new year", and the swap site was described as remaining open indefinitely. The **NFT** re-mint is documented as complete in December 2021; the date Phase 3 actually concluded is `# TODO`.

## 2022–2023 — build-out

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2022 | **Showrooms** evolve from display shelves into creative, themed environments, alongside AR sharing. |
| 2022–2023 | Catalog and licensor expansion; Pixar, additional Star Wars lines, and international artists join the platform. |

> [!note] Thin period
> VeVe's own retrospective compresses 2022–2023 into a single paragraph, and this section is correspondingly light. Specific 2022–2023 milestones (feature launches, licensor signings, corporate changes) are `# TODO` pending a further research pass. The drop record for these years is nonetheless dense — see [[sets/_index|Sets]] and [[collectibles/_index|Collectibles]].

## 2024 — VeVe Comics

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **14 Mar 2024** | **VeVe Comics launches**, with **Marvel Comics as the first publisher** and 300+ digital issues available on day one. New Marvel issues are added weekly, same-day as print. The launch release states VeVe had sold **over 10 million digital collectibles** to date, and cites panel-by-panel reading manually converted page by page. |

## 2025 — VeVeVerse, StackR, and a chain of its own

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 21 Feb 2025 | VeVe announces the VeVeVerse launch date. |
| **28 Feb 2025** | **VeVeVerse launches as an MVP** on desktop — shared 3D spaces where collectibles display life-sized and collectors meet by voice and text. |
| ~Apr 2025 | **VeVeVerse mobile** ships. |
| **28–29 Apr 2025** | **StackR goes live** ([stackr.world](https://stackr.world)). For the first time VeVe collectibles can be bought and sold **directly with cryptocurrency** — **[[OMI Token\|OMI]]**, which StackR accepts on **Base or Ethereum** — with purchases and sales reflected back into the user's VeVe collection. VeVe's own announcement (22 Apr 2025) gave 28 April; press coverage reports the integration going live on 29 April after "a year in beta testing". |
| **19 Nov 2025** | **Collect Chain announced** — *"Introducing Collect: The Next Era of Digital Collecting."* A purpose-built chain for collectibles with **royalties and rights embedded at the chain level**. Stated roadmap: a Collect website in **December 2025**, **Phase 1 migration completing January 2026**, and **Phase 2 optional self-custody** afterwards. Ownership, edition numbers, rarities and metadata carry over automatically; no user action required. |

## 2026 — migration complete

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Jan 2026 | Phase 1 of the Collect Chain migration was **scheduled** to complete. No announcement confirming it landed in January was located — the next confirmed datapoint is the 1 Apr 2026 completion post, so the actual Phase 1 date is `# TODO`. |
| **1 Apr 2026** | **VeVe announces the full migration to Collect Chain is complete.** A new block explorer, **collectscan.com**, ships alongside it for transaction and ownership history. VeVe's framing: *"only the underlying infrastructure has evolved."* |
| Post-migration | **Phase 2 — optional self-custody**, letting collectors hold collectibles in personal wallets, is planned but **undated**. |

## Chain lineage

| Chain | Period | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **GoChain** | 2020 – 2021 | Original minting chain; OMI issued as a GO20 token |
| **Immutable X** (Ethereum L2) | 2021 – 2026 | Gas-free minting/trading; OMI becomes ERC-20 (later also on Base) |
| **Collect Chain** | 2026 – | Purpose-built, chain-level royalties; explorer at collectscan.com |

## Season structure

VeVe groups drops into **Seasons**. Season 1 was explicitly the trial/beta era and closed with its final drop on **13 May 2021**. From Season 2 onward the catalog shows a consistent roughly six-month cadence, with new seasons opening around **May** and **November** each year, currently through **Season 11**.

| Season | Approx. window (from catalog drop dates) |
|---|---|
| 1 | Oct 2020 – May 2021 |
| 2 | May 2021 – Oct 2021 |
| 3 | Nov 2021 – Apr 2022 |
| 4 | May 2022 – Oct 2022 |
| 5 | Oct 2022 – May 2023 |
| 6 | May 2023 – Oct 2023 |
| 7 | Oct 2023 – Apr 2024 |
| 8 | May 2024 – Oct 2024 |
| 9 | Nov 2024 – May 2025 |
| 10 | May 2025 – Oct 2025 |
| 11 | Nov 2025 – present |

> [!note] How these windows were derived
> Season boundaries are **inferred** from the 5th–95th percentile of `nft_drop_date` across the **2,492 season-tagged** collectibles in this wiki (of 2,850 total — comics carry no `season`), not taken from an official season calendar. A handful of items carry season tags well outside their neighbours (re-drops, special editions, and later additions to older sets), so the ranges overlap slightly at the edges. VeVe has not published an authoritative season-boundary table; that remains `# TODO`.

## Where the record starts

This wiki's own market history is much younger than the platform. Real completed-sale data begins **2025-07-12** and now covers **300,000+ sales** across both markets — VeVe's in-app market in [[Gems]] and StackR in OMI. Legendary trades from the 2021 boom therefore sit outside the dataset and belong on curated history pages rather than in [[platform/record-sales|Record Sales]].

questions/how-do-mint-numbers-work.md:
# How Do Mint Numbers Work?

Every VeVe collectible is issued in a fixed edition, and every individual copy carries a unique **mint number** within it — "#41 of 1,200". Which one *you* get in a drop is random and not revealed until after purchase. Mint number is the only axis on which two otherwise-identical copies of the same collectible differ, and it is where collectors pay the steepest and least predictable premiums.

This page answers the mechanics (assignment, reserves, lowest public mint), the taxonomy of chased mints (catalogued in depth in [[Significant Mints]]), and — most importantly — what the premium measurably is rather than what collector lore says it is.

## 1. What a mint number is

- It is the **serial number of your copy** inside its edition: 1 … `totalIssued`. A collectible with 15,000 editions has mints #1–#15,000.
- It is **immutable and travels with the token**. Trading a copy does not renumber it.
- It is a property of your copy, **not of the collectible**. Rarity tier, edition size and mint number are three separate things — see [[platform/rarity-system]] for how each behaves.
- Comics carry mints too, but on a **shared** pool: all cover variants of one issue draw from a single 1…N sequence, so an issue has exactly one #1 and one ceiling mint across every cover. Collectibles are the opposite — each collectible in a set is numbered independently, so a five-piece set contains five #41s. Confirmed on-chain in this vault's reserve-wallet index: of 3,158 multi-cover issues, 3,019 hold editions that are fully disjoint across covers and 3,096 have exactly one cover holding #1.

## 2. How mints are assigned

Two different mechanisms, and conflating them is the most common misunderstanding:

| Stage | How the mint is determined |
|---|---|
| **Minting** | The order in which editions are written to the chain — `# TODO`, see callout. |
| **Primary drop / waitlist** | Rarity *and* edition number are **randomly allocated** to buyers, and "will not be known to you until you have completed the purchase and the collectible has been delivered." Being fast in the queue does not earn a low mint. |
| **Secondary market** | The mint number is **visible and chooseable** — "Each listing displays key details such as the collectible name, edition number, rarity tier, and listed price," so a buyer targeting #41 or #1111 shops for it directly and pays for it. |

> [!warning] Unverified — sequential minting
> The frequently repeated claim that editions are minted to the chain in strict sequence (#1 first, then #2, and so on) appears in no VeVe or Vevepedia page located during fact-check. Minting order is `# TODO`. Only the *allocation* to buyers is documented as random.

That split is why mint premiums exist only on the secondary side. In a drop, a low mint is a lottery outcome; on the market, it is a purchase decision, and price sorts accordingly.

## 3. Reserved editions: why #1 usually isn't for sale

VeVe holds a block of editions back from public sale. The official wording on drop pages is that a stated number "will be withheld by VeVe for licensor, promotional, team and comp distribution." The consequence: **the lowest mint you can buy is usually not #1.**

Across this vault's mirror of VeVe's own store data, **2,658 of 2,849 catalogued collectibles (93.3%) report a first publicly available edition**, and it takes **35 distinct values**:

| First public mint | Items | Share | Implied contiguous reserve |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **#41** | 1,397 | 52.6% | 40 |
| **#21** | 607 | 22.8% | 20 |
| **#1** | 165 | 6.2% | none |
| #6 | 164 | 6.2% | 5 |
| #11 | 106 | 4.0% | 10 |
| #42 | 42 | 1.6% | 41 |
| #31 | 35 | 1.3% | 30 |
| #16 | 31 | 1.2% | 15 |
| 27 other values | 111 | 4.2% | up to 192 |

So **#41 is the single most common answer and is right about half the time** — and roughly one item in sixteen has no reserve at all. Community references describe the #1–40 block as convention, and note it "was not always the case in the past and could change in the future."

> [!warning] Reserve counts vary per item — never assume #41
> Reserve depth is **not** inferable from rarity, edition size, or even from sibling items in the same set. A single verified drop, Disney·Pixar **UP Characters Series**, uses four different combinations at once:
>
> | Collectible | Rarity | Editions | Withheld | First public mint |
> |---|---|---:|---:|---:|
> | Carl Fredricksen | Uncommon | 2,009 | 90 | #41 |
> | Russell | Rare | 1,312 | 90 | #41 |
> | Charles Muntz | Ultra Rare | 409 | 40 | #21 |
> | Kevin | Secret Rare | 88 | 10 | #11 |
>
> Read the item's own first-available-edition field. Anything else is a guess.

### Withheld total ≠ the low block

Note the UP table: Charles Muntz withholds **40** editions but its first public mint is **#21** — so 20 sit in a contiguous low block and 20 are scattered **above** it. VeVe withholds random higher mints for marketing and giveaways as well as the low run.

This is visible on-chain. This project indexed the holdings of a single VeVe-controlled reserve wallet (identified as the second-largest holder of the VeVe ERC-721 collection, distinct from the store/unsold-inventory wallet): **419,772 held editions across 17,436 items**, snapshot 2026-07-08. **96.4% of indexed items have held editions above their contiguous low block.** Example — the Secret Rare *#01 Eduardo Risso Batman – Blue & Yellow Variant* holds #1–40 **plus** #864, #877, #880–881, #885–886 and dozens more scattered upward.

## 4. The lowest public mint (LPM)

The **LPM** is the lowest edition VeVe ever sold to the public — the practical floor of the "low mint" hunt for that item, because everything below it was never obtainable at drop. It is the number the community and this project's tooling treat as the real #1.

Two caveats that matter:

- **Reserved mints can still reach collectors.** Giveaways, licensor distribution and comps put sub-LPM editions into circulation, so a #12 on a #41-LPM item is not a data error. It is also the stated tail risk on low mints: if VeVe or a licensor released reserves in volume, sub-LPM scarcity would dilute.
- **Coverage is partial and hand-checked in part.** Exact LPMs come from VeVe's own store data where available; older and newer edges of the catalog are patchier. Treat any LPM claim on an item without a reported value as unknown, not as #41.

## 5. Which mints collectors chase

The full taxonomy — with the character-specific year lists — lives in [[Significant Mints]]. In summary:

| Family | Examples | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Lowest public mint** | the item's LPM (#41, #21, #11 …) | the true "first" a collector can own |
| **Low mints** | #1, single digits, sub-50, sub-100 | conventional scarcity; sub-100 is the usual dividing line |
| **Ceiling / high mints** | `#` = edition size, near-ceiling | one per edition; prized especially on comics |
| **Repdigits & patterns** | #111, #2222, #1212 | one-of-a-kind within the run |
| **Palindromes** | #1331, #12321 | numismatic crossover ("fancy serials") |
| **Runs** | #123, #1234, #9876 | ascending / descending sequences |
| **Year mints** | #1939 (Batman's debut), #1962, #1977 | must be *meaningful to that character* to command anything |
| **Milestones / round numbers** | #1000, #5000, #100 | milestone psychology |
| **Meme numbers** | #69, #420, #666, #1337 | pure internet demand |
| **Lore numbers** | #616 on Marvel items (Earth-616) | franchise-specific in-jokes |

## 6. What the premium actually is

> [!warning] Measurement caveat — read before the tables
> This project's mirror of **302,286 completed market sales since 2025-07-12** records collectible, date and price — but **not the mint number of the copy that sold.** Real completed sales therefore *cannot* be attributed to a mint number directly. The multiples below are measured on the **ask side**: 27,723 active listings (VeVe in Gems + StackR in OMI, converted to USD), snapshot 2026-07-30, which *do* carry mint numbers. Asks are what sellers want, not what buyers paid, and [[platform/floor-prices|floor prices]] on illiquid items are notoriously troll-priced. Read these as the shape and rank order of the premium, not as an appraisal.

Method: restricted to the **1,374 collectibles with at least 8 active listings** (22,880 listings). Each listing is expressed as a multiple of **that same collectible's median ask**, so the comparison is copy-vs-copy inside one edition — the only difference between them is the mint number. Medians reported, because the tail is wild.

### By absolute mint number

| Mint band | Listings | Median ask multiple | 75th pct |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| #1–10 | 26 | 2.00× | 3.08× |
| **#11–50** | 730 | **3.42×** | 10.00× |
| **#51–100** | 1,440 | **2.72×** | 6.96× |
| #101–500 | 4,515 | 1.01× | 2.00× |
| #501–1,000 | 3,934 | 1.00× | 1.71× |
| #1,001+ | 12,235 | 1.00× | 1.53× |

The premium is **sharply concentrated under #100 and effectively gone above ~#500**. The #1–10 row is thin (n=26) because almost all of those editions are reserved and never listed.

### By position within the edition

Absolute mint means little without edition size — #300 is nothing on a 15,000-run and near-legendary on a 350-run.

| Position in edition | Listings | Median ask multiple | 75th pct |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| bottom 1% | 190 | **13.82×** | 48.99× |
| 1–5% | 1,537 | 3.22× | 7.67× |
| 5–25% | 4,784 | 1.24× | 2.98× |
| middle 25–75% | 10,479 | 1.00× | 1.43× |
| 75–99% | 5,528 | 0.95× | 1.15× |
| top 1% | 362 | 2.80× | 16.29× |
| **ceiling mint** (`#` = edition size) | 86 | **25.47×** | 118.36× |

Two readings: the curve is **U-shaped** — asks rise at both ends and the cheapest copies of any collectible sit in its upper-middle. And the ceiling-mint figure, while the largest in the dataset, rests on 86 listings of a one-per-edition item that sellers can price at anything; treat it as directional.

### Relative to the lowest public mint

Restricted to the 1,337 eligible items with a known LPM (22,316 listings):

| Position | Listings | Median ask multiple | 75th pct |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **exactly the LPM** | 69 | **14.22×** | 58.57× |
| LPM+1 … LPM+9 | 315 | 4.33× | 12.14× |
| LPM+10 … LPM+59 | 1,396 | 2.75× | 7.02× |

The LPM itself is the single most expensive ordinary position in the whole dataset — the "true #1" premium is real and it is steep. Only 4 listings in the sample sat *below* an item's LPM (escaped reserves), too few to quantify.

### Pattern mints vs. a matched control

Control group: mints sitting in the 25–99% band of their edition (n=16,007, median **0.98×**) — i.e. ordinary mints with no low-mint effect. Pattern mints *within that same band*, so the multiple below is the pattern effect alone:

| Pattern | Listings | Median ask multiple | 75th pct |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| round thousands (#1000, #2000) | 80 | **8.07×** | 17.17× |
| meme numbers (#69, #420, #666, #1337) | 59 | **5.04×** | 16.67× |
| repdigits (#111, #2222) | 228 | 3.69× | 14.38× |
| year mints (1900–2026) | 806 | 3.57× | 15.00× |
| ascending runs (#123, #1234) | 124 | 3.43× | 9.95× |
| multiples of 100 (#100, #500 — includes the round-thousands row above) | 288 | 1.95× | 7.03× |
| descending runs (#321, #9876) | 104 | 1.85× | 5.14× |
| palindromes (3+ digits) | 853 | 1.12× | 3.27× |
| *(control: ordinary mid-edition mints)* | 16,007 | 0.98× | 1.33× |

The surprise is **palindromes**, the most-hyped family in the numismatic-crossover argument, asking barely above control at the median. Round thousands and meme numbers ask the most. Year mints ask well, but this measurement counts *any* 1900–2026 number and cannot tell whether the year is meaningful to that character — the premium for a meaningful year is presumably higher and for an arbitrary one lower.

### What completed sales can still tell us

Sale records lack mints, but every copy of one collectible is otherwise identical, so **price dispersion inside a single collectible over a single month** bounds the mint effect. Across the **3,151 collectible-months with at least 20 recorded sales** (194,455 sales):

| Measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Top sale ÷ median sale, same item, same month (median case) | **4.23×** |
| Same, 75th percentile | 9.97× |
| Same, 90th percentile | 33.33× |
| Share of sales printing ≥10× their item-month median | **1.15%** |
| Collectible-months containing at least one 5×+ sale | 44.7% |
| Collectible-months containing at least one 10×+ sale | 24.8% |

So roughly **one sale in ninety prints at 10× or more than what the same collectible was fetching that month** — that population is where special mints trade, and its size is consistent with the ask-side picture. It is an upper bound, not a pure measurement: bidding wars, bundles and mistakes live in the same tail. This is also why the vault's own market tooling deliberately **excludes premium-serial sales** when computing an edition's price level — a #41 selling for $4,000 does not mean ordinary copies are worth $4,000.

> [!warning] Unverified — the widely-quoted multiples
> Community reference material states sub-100 premiums over floor of roughly **10× (Common), 8× (Uncommon), 6× (Rare), 4× (Ultra Rare), 3× (Secret Rare)**, and **20–30× for sub-50**. The ask-side measurement here is **directionally consistent but materially smaller**: bottom-5%-of-edition asks run 2.96×–3.98× by tier, and sub-50 asks run 1.66×–4.99× by tier. The two are not measuring the same thing (median ask vs. lowest ask, and different item mixes), and neither is a completed-sale measurement. Do not use either as a valuation.

### By rarity tier

Same method, split by tier. "Low" = bottom 5% of the edition; "control" = the 25–99% band of the same tier.

| Rarity | Low-mint listings | Median low-mint multiple | Control multiple | Sub-50 asks |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Common | 692 | 3.76× | 1.00× | 3.53× (n=196) |
| Uncommon | 377 | 3.35× | 0.96× | 4.98× (n=86) |
| Rare | 357 | 3.98× | 0.96× | 4.99× (n=112) |
| Ultra Rare | 201 | 3.17× | 0.95× | 4.11× (n=148) |
| Secret Rare | 100 | 2.96× | 0.96× | 1.66× (n=214) |

The **low-mint multiple shrinks as rarity rises** — clearest at Secret Rare, whose sub-50 asks are only 1.66× its own median. The intuition holds: on a 355-edition median Secret Rare, scarcity is already priced into every copy, so the mint number has less left to add. On a 2,000-edition Common, the mint number is nearly the whole story.

## 7. Mint numbers and Master Collector Points

Low mints are the one mint category with a **mechanical, published payoff** rather than a purely market one. Per the official [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] rules:

- **Collectibles:** **+0.5** points/day — verbatim: "Points earned for the 5% lowest mints available to the public (total editions *0.05%),(excludes any Collectibles retained by VeVe)".
- **Comics:** **+50%** on that comic's points — verbatim: "50% Points earned for the 5% lowest mint Comic available to the public (total editions *0.05%), (excludes any Comics retained by VeVe)."

> [!warning] Unverified — which base the 5% is taken from
> VeVe's published wording is self-inconsistent: it says "available to the public" but states the formula as `total editions * 0.05`. Whether the bonus band is 5% of the printed edition size or 5% of the *public* run — and therefore whether an item's reserve depth shifts where the threshold falls — is `# TODO`.

Patterns, palindromes, year mints and ceiling mints earn **nothing** in MCP — no such bonus appears anywhere in the published point table, so their value is entirely market sentiment.

## 8. Practical rules of thumb

1. **Read the item's own first-available-edition value.** #41 is a coin flip, not a rule.
2. **Judge a mint as a percentage of its edition,** not as an absolute number.
3. **The LPM is the premium position**; the rest of the low band decays fast, and past ~#500 or the 25% mark the mint number stops mattering to price.
4. **The cheapest copy of anything sits in the 75–99% band** — the upper-middle of the run asks below the item's own median.
5. **Low mints beat pattern mints for reliability.** Only low mints pay MCP; patterns depend entirely on finding a buyer who wants that number.
6. **Ignore any single headline sale.** Within-item dispersion means a special-mint print says nothing about ordinary copies.
7. **Reserve release is the structural risk** on low mints, and nothing about it is under a collector's control.

## Sources

- https://www.vevepedia.com/terms/mint-number/
- https://www.vevepedia.com/terms/low-mint/
- https://www.vevepedia.com/terms/rarity/
- https://www.veve.me/blog/veve/101/veve-waitlist-drops-what-you-need-to-know/
- https://www.veve.me/blog/collectibles/disney-pixar-up-characters-series/
- https://www.veve.me/blog/veve/mcp/veve-master-collector-program-earning-mcp-points/
- https://www.veve.me/blog/news/how-the-veve-nft-marketplace-works/ — listings display the edition number
- https://vevemintfinder.medium.com/understanding-comic-book-covers-in-veve-e4bc123159da — comic mint numbering is shared across all cover rarities (one #1 per issue)
- https://gocollect.com/blog/comparing-veve-fancy-mints-with-real-world-number-collecting
- https://www.veve.me/blog/collectibles/automobili-lamborghini-350-gt/
- Internal: `app/data/all_listings.js` — 27,723 active listings across 2,511 collectibles (VeVe + StackR), snapshot 2026-07-30 09:40 UTC (all ask-side multiples)
- Internal: `tools/market_sales_cache.jsonl` — 302,286 completed sales since 2025-07-12 (dispersion figures); see [[platform/record-sales]]
- Internal: `app/data/catalog.js` — 2,849 catalogued collectibles, 2,658 with a reported first public edition (LPM distribution)
- Internal: `app/data/held.js` — on-chain index of VeVe's reserve wallet, 419,772 held editions across 17,436 items, snapshot 2026-07-08
